Databases.title: A Multimodal Type 2 Diabetes Registry on DHIS2: A Design and Feasibility Study with the AI-READI Dataset
Databases.summary: Care for type 2 diabetes increasingly draws on continuous glucose monitors, wearable devices, home sensors, clinical records and retinal images, yet few open platforms have been shown to hold all of these for the same person. We asked three questions of DHIS2, the open-source health information system that ministries of health in about 80 countries run nationally: whether an unmodified Tracker program can represent these modalities together (RQ1), which design choices its row-per-event data model forces for dense sensor streams (RQ2), and what a bulk loader must do to load such data correctly (RQ3). We designed a registry of 27 program stages and 445 data elements, loaded the AI-READI dataset of 2,280 participants into it, and verified the result field by field against the source files. The program held every loaded modality in 8.09 million events. Dense streams were stored as hourly summaries aligned across modalities; electrocardiograms, diagnoses and 118,480 retinal images were stored as one event per record. The event model ruled out storing raw readings, and hourly summaries reduced the wearable and glucose volume about 26-fold. An audit of the loader found defects that shared one pattern: a failure that looked like success. We state five lessons for DHIS2 Tracker clients that address this pattern. Verification of all 64.9 million stored values found four defects, all missing, duplicated or artifactual records rather than wrong values, and none after their repair; an independent recomputation of the glucose summaries agreed on all 464,210 values compared. The paper offers implementation guidance for DHIS2 implementers and for users of AI-READI; it does not evaluate clinical use. Analytics at this scale, use by clinicians and live device feeds remain to be shown.

Databases.title: CypherGuard: Database-Grounded Correction for Reliable Text-to-Cypher
Databases.summary: Text-to-Cypher translates natural-language questions into Cypher queries over property graphs. Graph database systems increasingly adopt this translation as a native query interface. Large language models generate fluent Cypher but stay unreliable. On Cypher-Bench a small model answers only 31.4% of questions correctly, and even a strong model plateaus at 71.76%. The dominant failure modes are structural rather than linguistic. For example, a generated query may parse correctly and follow the schema, yet still return zero rows because it traverses a relationship against the stored graph direction. To address this issue, we present CypherGuard, a training-free framework that detects and corrects these structural faults. Our approach uses two core components: a graph-native error taxonomy to guide repair, and a mined rule library to guide query generation. At inference time, CypherGuard first rewrites schema-detectable faults, then re-executes each draft and repairs it only when the query errors or returns nothing. On CypherBench test questions, across seven graphs, CypherGuard reaches 88.50% overall execution accuracy, +25.08% over the same-backbone zero-shot floor, surpassing an RL-fine-tuned 7B specialist and the strongest training-based system that we compare against.

Databases.title: Tessera: Fast Join-Aggregates over Skewed Sparse Relations in Database Engines
Databases.summary: Join-aggregate queries count or sum matching rows for each pair of values, often over skewed sparse relations in which a few values are frequent and most pairs of values never co-occur. Conventional execution plans materialize billions of intermediate join rows, taking minutes to tens of minutes per query. Recent matrix-based solutions reformulate these queries as matrix multiplication to reduce or avoid this materialization. However, they remain slow because they either store result cells for non-matching pairs or still materialize intermediate join rows for infrequent values. We present Tessera, a skew-aware join-aggregate operator for database engines that avoids both sources of overhead. Specifically, Tessera computes a sparse matrix product directly over the engine's rows, emits only nonzero cells as result rows, and prunes values that cannot meet the query's threshold before multiplication begins. It also offloads the dense block formed by pairs of the most frequent values to a CPU matrix accelerator when that block is dense enough. Experimental results show that Tessera is faster than the fastest existing system by 2.8x to 18.8x. In addition, Tessera outperforms DuckDB's execution plans by up to 1,802x.

Databases.title: Towards Universal Tabular Embeddings: A Benchmark Across Data Tasks
Databases.summary: Tabular foundation models aim to learn universal representations of tabular data that transfer across tasks and domains, enabling applications such as table retrieval, semantic search and table-based prediction. Despite the growing number of such models, it remains unclear which approach works best in practice, as existing methods are often evaluated under task-specific settings that make direct comparison difficult. To address this, we introduce TEmBed, the Tabular Embedding Test Bed, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating tabular embeddings across four representation levels: cell, row, column, and table. Evaluating a diverse set of tabular representation learning models, we show that which model to use depends on the task and representation level. Our results offer practical guidance for selecting tabular embeddings in real-world applications and lay the groundwork for developing more general-purpose tabular representation models.

Databases.title: Supervised and LLM-Augmented Cardinality Estimation for Similarity Queries on Knowledge Graphs
Databases.summary: Over the past decades, query cardinality estimation on relational databases has been proven crucial, enabling the result size estimation of all sub-plans of each query. This allowed query optimizers to design efficient query plans, towards minimizing the query response time. Lately, knowledge graphs are being preferred over traditional databases in various applications, due to their ability to represent complex relationships and semantic meaning in a domain-specific context. In this work, we present a novel approach for supervised similarity-aware cardinality estimation on knowledge graphs that incorporates similarities into the model training process, thus treating them as first-class citizens. To this end, we present SCE-KG, a model that employs a novel encoding scheme for cardinality estimation, named SGsplit. We further extend our approach by leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate training queries that resemble realistic user workloads, and show that combining LLM-generated and random walk samples consistently improves estimation accuracy on test workloads generated by two independent LLMs. Our experimental evaluation reveals that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques in terms of prediction error, achieving 40x and 37x improvement for star and chain queries, respectively (95th percentile), whereas its online overhead accounts for less than 0.05% of the average query execution time and less than 1% of the average query planning time, showing a sub-millisecond latency in all cases.

Databases.title: Fidelity Synopses: Pre-Execution Plan Selection for Approximate Vector Search
Databases.summary: Vector search has become a database operator with many physical implementations: different index families, build-time and search-time parameters, and compressed or disk-resident variants. Each trades cost against fidelity, the fraction of a query's exact top-k nearest neighbors that a configuration returns. Deployments nevertheless choose one configuration offline and use it for every query, so they are sized for their hardest queries and overpay for the rest. On a 5.8M-item LAION benchmark with four embedding models, running each query on the cheapest configuration that suffices for it would roughly halve the cost in a typical setting. Exploiting this requires predicting each configuration's fidelity before running it, which is hard because fidelity is defined by the very exact search that approximate indexes avoid. Relational optimizers solve the analogous problem for cardinality with offline synopses; we propose one for vector search. A fidelity synopsis divides the embedding space into cells around a set of landmarks and records, for every cell and configuration, how often that configuration met a fidelity target on a sample of queries. At query time, one nearest-landmark lookup yields a calibrated estimate for every configuration, and an optimizer chooses configurations so that the workload misses the target no more often than its requirement allows. We test the two premises the synopsis relies on, that fidelity varies smoothly across the embedding space and that its loss is specific to each configuration. Held to the same requirement a static deployment is built to meet, synopsis-guided selection lowers cost in all 16 combinations of model and query direction, to a median of 0.72x the static deployment, with a batched lookup of 21-32 microseconds per query. The saving persists against the best static choice among the same indexes, and within a single index at no extra memory.

Databases.title: Open Biomedical Knowledge Graphs at Scale: Construction, Federation, and AI Agent Access with Samyama Graph Database
Databases.summary: Biomedical knowledge is fragmented across siloed databases---Reactome, STRING, Gene Ontology, ClinicalTrials.gov, DrugBank, DGIdb, SIDER, PubMed, ClinVar, ChEMBL, OpenTargets, and more. We present an open, reproducible biomedical knowledge graph ecosystem built on Samyama, a Rust-native graph database: three foundational graphs detailed end-to-end---Pathways KG (118,686 nodes, 834,785 edges), Clinical Trials KG (7,774,446 nodes, 26,973,997 edges), and Drug Interactions KG (32,726 nodes, 191,970 edges)---and their expansion into a 22-graph, 2-cohort merged biomedical store (328,130,739 nodes and 1,441,425,733 imported edges, including 295,000 synthetic OMOP CDM patients from Synthea). First, we describe a reproducible ETL and portable .sgsnap snapshot pattern where graphs load alone or compose into one store. Second, we analyze single-store cross-KG integration via query-time property joins and load-time identifier deduplication (--dedup-keys): across all 24 snapshots (Samyama-Graph v1.13.0), 328.1M nodes and 1.44B edges load in 2,269.1 s (37m 49s) within 366.5 GB peak RSS (254 B/edge), merging 132,511 cross-source entities across five audited keys (mondo_id,uniprot_id,go_id,drugbank_id,symbol)---87.8% of the 150,965 Bound A sound-identifier ceiling, with zero conflicting-ID refusals. On a frozen 81-query suite, 62 queries return results (17 data-gap empties, 2 timeouts); on an expanded 200-query oracle suite, 195 of 200 pass (97.5%). Third, we introduce schema-driven Model Context Protocol (MCP) server generation: on the 40-question BiomedQA benchmark over the 3-KG subset, domain-specific MCP tools achieve 98% accuracy vs. 85% for schema-aware text-to-Cypher and 75% for standalone GPT-4o, with zero schema errors.
Databases.comment: 14 pages, 9 tables. v4 adds 22-KG + 2-cohort (328.1M nodes, 1.44B edges) single-store merge on Samyama-Graph v1.13.0, Bound A identifier soundness audit (132,511 merges), and 200-query oracle suite (195/200 pass). Code and benchmarks: https://github.com/samyama-ai/biomedqa

Databases.title: Recommendation Systems for Exploratory Data Tasks
Databases.summary: Exploratory Data Tasks (EDTs) involve iteratively steering workflows as users refine their subjective goals based on newly emerging insights. EDTs are performed by millions of users with varying levels of expertise to understand unfamiliar data, discover trends, and identify evidence that informs critical decision-making. However, a key challenge in EDTs is the enormous space of possible actions that one can take at each step: users struggle to choose among thousands of joins, transformations, and aggregations, leading to exploration paralysis. Because EDT workflows are interconnected, each choice shapes subsequent exploration, and suboptimal choices can lead to inefficiency, missed insights, confirmation bias, and incomplete coverage. This calls for intelligent recommendations that efficiently guide users toward optimal EDT actions. We envision recommendation as a core capability of data systems, proactively guiding users toward promising actions that lower the barrier to EDTs. This capability becomes even more critical as AI agents emerge as a new class of users that perform EDTs on behalf of humans. EDT recommendation is challenging because the action space is combinatorial and actions are data-dependent, which require costly materialization. Moreover, recommendation often involves bundles or sequences of actions across interdependent tasks, requiring coordination across tasks. In this paper, we present our vision of EDT recommendation systems along two axes: single-task vs. multi-task settings and single-action vs. multi-action recommendations. We outline a research agenda that progresses from recommending individual EDT actions to constrained bundles and sequences of actions, and ultimately to coordinated recommendations across interconnected EDTs. We identify research directions for incorporating various contexts, addressing efficiency challenges, and coordinating across tasks.

Databases.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
Databases.summary: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.

Databases.title: Blockchain-Based Privacy-Preserving Data Management
Databases.summary: Privacy-preservation policies are guidelines formulated to protect data providers private data. Previous privacy-preservation methodologies have addressed privacy in which data are permanently stored in repositories and disconnected from changing data provider privacy preferences. This occurrence becomes evident as data moves to another data repository. Hence, the need for data providers to control and flexibly update their existing privacy preferences due to changing data usage continues to remain a problem. This paper proposes a blockchain-based methodology for preserving data provider's private and sensitive data. The research proposes to tightly couple data provider's private attribute data element to privacy preferences and data accessor data element into a privacy tuple. The implementation presents a framework of tightly-coupled relational database and blockchains. This delivers secure, tamper-resistant, and query-efficient platform for data management and query processing. The evaluation analysis from the implementation validates efficient query processing of privacy-aware queries on the privacy infrastructure. Moreover, a comparative analysis to other methodology approaches indicates that our approach offers efficient and better technique for data provider's private data protection and identity preservation.
Databases.comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables

Databases.title: SpBench: An Agent-Native Framework for Cross-Engine Lakehouse Benchmarking
Databases.summary: SpBench is an agent-native framework for cross-engine lakehouse benchmarking, in production use for benchmarking Snowpark, Snowpark Connect for Apache Spark, and other execution environments across standardized suites -- such as TPCx-BB and TPC-DI -- and custom benchmarks distilled from production workload patterns. It runs continuously across a broad portfolio of workloads, guiding the performance roadmap and detecting regressions for production-scale data engines. Benchmarking has historically been an expensive investment requiring continuous cross-functional collaboration and domain expertise, making it difficult to obtain actionable performance insights. SpBench provides (i) a typed, code-generated benchmark substrate that compiles platform-agnostic benchmark definitions into fair, comparable platform-specific implementations; (ii) a structured-telemetry contract recording every run as queryable fact and dimension data, letting LLM agents query results deterministically; and (iii) an agent-native harness of three composable skills to expedite building benchmarks and analyzing results. This agent-native architecture enabled the rapid development of more than 400 benchmark queries that run on a regular cadence to detect performance regressions; catching these has directly led to improvements in production.
Databases.comment: 4 pages, 4 figures. To appear at IEEE BigData 2026. Lyndon Shi, Nic Crouch, Yi Hu, and Zihao Ye contributed equally

Databases.title: Not All Neighbors Matter: Understanding the Impact of Graph Sparsification on GNN Pipelines
Databases.summary:
As graphs scale to billions of nodes and edges, graph Machine Learning workloads are constrained by the cost of multi-hop traversals over exponentially growing neighborhoods. While various system-level and algorithmic optimizations have been proposed to accelerate Graph Neural Network (GNN) pipelines, data management and movement remain the primary bottlenecks at scale. In this paper, we explore whether graph sparsification, a well-established technique that reduces edges to create sparser neighborhoods, can serve as a lightweight pre-processing step to address these bottlenecks while preserving model quality.
  We develop an extensible experimental framework that integrates graph sparsification into GNN training and inference pipelines, and use it to study how four representative sparsification methods interact with four GNN architectures, across six graphs and two learning tasks (node classification and link prediction). Our central finding is counter-intuitive: removing a large fraction of a graph's edges, often the majority, has only a small effect on model quality, and sometimes improves it. For example, the K-Neighbor sparsifier removes 83.3% of the edges of the Products graph while GCN accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points, and on the Arxiv link prediction task, sparsification raises GraphSAGE test AUC from 0.86 to 0.95. Because the runtime costs scale with the number of edges, these reductions translate into substantial speedups. Our results show that the pre-processing overhead is quickly amortized, making sparsification practical even for very large graphs.

Databases.title: A Formal Diagnostic Framework for Graph Repair Systems
Databases.summary: Graph-based data representations excel at capturing relations among entities, e.g., for semantic web, artificial intelligence, or database applications, and their utility depends critically on their quality, usually enforced via graph schemas. These schemas are often violated, e.g., during data ingestion, calling for repair actions to achieve compliance. This paper presents a formal diagnostic framework for graph repair methods. Current methods often lack rigor and generality, since they rely on ad hoc test datasets. Our method starts, instead, from a compliant graph and uses an abstract rewriting system to systematically introduce schema violations while ensuring provable coverage of the constraints in the schema. We apply the framework to several repair methods, including those based on large language models, and assess their performance across multiple metrics. Results show that our framework effectively differentiates the performance of different methods across various constraints, highlighting the importance of fine-grained, systematic tools for graph repair.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Turnstile Streaming Algorithms Might (Still) as Well Be Linear Sketches, for Polynomial-Length Streams
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A fundamental question in streaming complexity is whether every space-efficient turnstile algorithm is implicitly a linear sketch. The work of Li, Nguyen, and Woodruff (STOC~2014) established an equivalence between the two, but their reduction requires a stream length that is at least doubly exponential in the dimension $n$. In the opposite direction, Kallaugher and Price (STOC~2020) showed a separation for streams of linear length, so the equivalence does not hold in general. The most natural and practically relevant regime, that of polynomial-length streams, has therefore remained open.
  We show that polynomial-length turnstile algorithms admit linear-sketch simulations. More precisely, if a turnstile algorithm uses $S$ bits of space and succeeds on all streams of length $\textrm{poly}(D, n)$, then on final vectors $x$ with $\|x\|_2 \le D$, its output can be recovered from $O(S)$ linear measurements of $x$, using $O(S)$ bits overall. For smooth problems under appropriate input distributions, a mollified version of the reduction yields a bounded-entry sketch with $O(S / \log D)$ measurements and optimal $O(S)$ total space. Our results extend to strict turnstile streams and non-uniform Read-Once Branching Programs (ROBPs).
  Instead of the transition-graph arguments of prior work, our proof uses Fourier analysis and tools from additive combinatorics to extract discrete linear measurements. We show that an $S$-bit algorithm can only be sensitive to a small set of heavy Fourier frequencies, which lie close to a finite group of order $2^{O(S)}$, and we use generators of this group as the rows of the sketching matrix. Combined with existing lower bounds for real sketches and for communication, this gives new lower bounds for polynomial-length turnstile streams.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Nearly Quadratic Lower Bound for Linear Optimization over Convex Bodies in the Membership Oracle Model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove nearly quadratic lower bounds for randomized algorithms for linear optimization and uniform sampling over convex bodies in the membership oracle model. For linear optimization, this matches the known nearly quadratic upper bound up to a polylog factor in the dimension. For uniform sampling, this improves on the previous linear lower bound. Our construction also implies the same lower bound for volume estimation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Pareto Secretary Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Pareto secretary problem asks for online selection of a Pareto-maximal observation from an i.i.d. sample: no other observation is at least as good in every coordinate and strictly better in one. For every fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and independent continuous coordinates, the optimal failure probability is of order $1/[(\log n)^{d-1}\log\log n]$, both with full information and with coordinate ranks alone. A deterministic rank rule attains the optimal leading term uniformly over the marginals. For every fixed positive definite Gaussian covariance, the same failure order holds, with a leading constant depending on the correlation matrix, and a rank-based rule attains the optimal leading failure probability without knowing the Gaussian parameters. In both models, we determine the optimal fixed cutoff and its leading failure constant; its failure probability exceeds the unrestricted optimum by a factor $Θ_d((\log\log n)^2)$. Under arbitrary dependence, a fixed joint density with uniform marginals can instead have optimal full-information success tending to approximately $0.58$. The proof uses the scarcity of observations with very small domination probability to bound every stopping rule. A matching rule selects a currently maximal point when this probability is below a threshold that increases as time runs out. Coordinate ranks from an initial sample provide sufficiently accurate estimates to preserve the optimal leading failure probability. For singular Gaussian distributions with known correlations, we characterize the optimal failure asymptotics attainable using ranks. Singular dependence can make every observation acceptable or recover the difficulty of selecting a single best point.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 48 pages, 8 figures. A preliminary version has been accepted to WINE 2026

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Capacitated Clustering with Few Extra Centers
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In capacitated $(k,z)$-clustering, we open $k$ centers and assign every client to a center within its capacity, minimizing the sum of $z$-th powers of the distances; $k$-median and $k$-means are the cases $z=1$ and $z=2$. We study polynomial-time algorithms that open $k+\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ centers but respect the capacities exactly. All ratios hold up to an additive $δ$ for every fixed $δ>0$.
  For uniform soft capacities in low dimensions, we obtain ratio $β-(β-1)\varepsilon$, where $β=3^z$ if the clients or the locations have bounded doubling dimension, and $β=\mathcal{B}_z<3^z$ for $z>1$ if the clients do and centers may lie anywhere in $\mathbb{R}^d$. This gives $3-2\varepsilon$ for $k$-median and $5-4\varepsilon$ for Euclidean $k$-means. We also obtain ratios bounded by a constant for hard capacities, and $1+(3^z-1)e^{-\varepsilon}$ for non-uniform soft capacities. These are the first polynomial-time ratios with $(1+\varepsilon)k$ centers that are bounded by a constant, apart from uniform $k$-median in the plane. For uniform $k$-median in general metrics, we obtain $3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ with soft and $7+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ with hard capacities, improving the previous $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
  Splitting the clusters of a near-optimal uncapacitated solution into groups of at most $U$ clients, where $U$ is the capacity, gives fewer than $2k$ groups. With fewer centers, groups must share centers. Each extra center gives private centers to about two groups, since a center of an optimal solution that serves only such groups can be closed. Thus $\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ extra centers remove almost an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the extra cost caused by sharing.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$.
  In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data.
  We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/α)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/α^2)$ random directions guarantees $α$ Sliced Wasserstein error.
  Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Implicit Additively Weighted Geodesic Voronoi Diagrams and Applications
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $m$ vertices. After $O(m)$-time preprocessing of $P$, for any set $S$ of $n$ additively weighted point sites, we compute an implicit additively weighted geodesic Voronoi diagram in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time, supporting nearest-neighbor queries in $O(\log(n+m))$ time. In contrast, explicitly constructing the diagram requires $Ω(m)$ time. Our algorithm introduces a new sweep-line paradigm that avoids explicitly constructing the diagram, together with a novel technique for point location in implicit subdivisions.
  As applications, we obtain new dynamic data structures for additively weighted geodesic nearest-neighbor searching and the first efficient algorithms for shortest paths in geodesic disk graphs. After the same $O(m)$-time preprocessing, single-source shortest paths in a geodesic disk graph of $n$ sites can be computed in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time in the unweighted case and $O(n^{3/2}(\log n+\log^2 m))$ time in the weighted case. We also extend our techniques to implicit farthest geodesic Voronoi diagrams for unweighted sites, obtaining analogous bounds and dynamic farthest-neighbor data structures.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $ρ=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $κ_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $κ_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $Ω(ρ^4/\logρ)$ classical queries but only $Θ(ρ)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Two choices suffice: $k$-out sampling leaves $O(n/k)$ intercomponent edges for $k\geq 2$
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Given a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices, random $k$-out sampling forms a spanning subgraph by having each vertex independently choose $k$ incident edges uniformly with replacement. We prove that, for every integer $k\geq2$, the expected number of original edges joining distinct sampled components is $O(n/k)$.
  This resolves the conjecture of Holm, King, Thorup, Zamir, and Zwick in its full range, improving their logarithmic sampling requirement to the optimal threshold of two choices per vertex. The bound fails for $k=1$, and the dependence $O(n/k)$ is tight up to constant factors. Our result holds with replacement and consequently also without replacement. In particular, this implies that contracting just two independent local choices per vertex suffices to reduce an arbitrary simple graph to a quotient with $O(n)$ edges in expectation, which is crucial in reducing the instance size for many contraction-based algorithms.
  Our proof uses switching arguments to relate intercomponent edges to bridges and a degree-weighted component potential, whose expectation we also bound with a switching argument.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation Problem (WCAP), we are given a $k$-edge-connected graph on $n$ vertices and a set of additional edges, called links, with nonnegative costs. Pairs of vertices arrive one by one, and an online algorithm must immediately and irrevocably buy links so that each pair becomes $(k+1)$-edge-connected. The goal is to minimize the total cost of the purchased links.
  We obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for WCAP, improving the previous $O(\log^2 n)$ bound (SODA 2026). Our bound is asymptotically optimal, even for randomized algorithms in the random-order model. The general problem reduces to the case where the underlying graph is a cycle, for which link costs in $\{0,1\}$ already yield an $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound. Surprisingly, for unit costs on a cycle, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $4$-competitive algorithm, improving the previous $O(\log n)$ bound (SODA 2026), and prove that this ratio is optimal among deterministic algorithms. Thus, with unit costs, cycles are easier than trees, where the optimal competitive ratio is $Θ(\log n)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: 3SUM Made Simpler (Without Matrix Multiplication), $k$-SUM Hypothesis Refuted for Odd $k$, and Real 3SUM/APSP Derandomized
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Recently, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem and a truly subcubic algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem were found by Anthropic, as reported by Alman and Vassilevska Williams (2026). These algorithms relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries, which was obtained by modifying known matrix multiplication techniques of Schönhage (1981) and Coppersmith (1982).
  1. We present a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs. It completely avoids the use of matrix multiplication but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion--exclusion (and does not even require fast Fourier transform), and so is conceptually easier to understand (the whole solution is about 5 pages long).
  2. Following a similar approach, we obtain a randomized algorithm for $k$-SUM for integer inputs for odd constant $k$ in $O(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil-\varepsilon_k})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon_k>0$, disproving the $k$-SUM Hypothesis for all odd $k$.
  3. Existing reductions from 3SUM and APSP to selected-entries rectangular matrix multiplication were randomized in the case of real-valued input. We present new deterministic reductions, yielding a truly subquadratic deterministic algorithm for Real 3SUM and a truly subcubic deterministic algorithm for Real APSP.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The C-3PO Framework: Algorithms for $\#\mathrm{BIS}$-Hard Problems on Graphs with Low Threshold Rank or High Girth
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give approximate counting and sampling algorithms for spin models on graphs of low threshold rank or high girth. Given any $n$-vertex graph $G$, let $k_η= k_η(G)$ count normalized-Laplacian eigenvalues strictly below $η$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-approximate counting algorithm outputs an estimate $\widehat Z$ of the partition function $Z$ satisfying $(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z$ with probability at least $3/4$. An $\varepsilon$-approximate sampling algorithm outputs a configuration whose distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the target distribution. We give the following results:
  (a) Ferromagnetic Potts. Fix $q\ge2$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $β_0(q,η)$ such that, for every inverse temperature $β\geβ_0$, the zero-field $q$-state Potts model admits approximate counting and sampling algorithms: (i) On arbitrary graphs in time $\exp(O(k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) Fix $Δ\ge 3$. On $Δ$-regular graphs of girth $g$ in time $\exp(O(n e^{-g})) \operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$
  (b) Bipartite hard-core. Fix $Δ\ge3$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $λ_0(Δ,η)$ such that, for every fugacity $λ\geλ_0$, the hard-core model admits approximate counting and sampling: (i) On $Δ$-regular vertex-transitive bipartite graphs in time $\exp(O (k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) On $Δ$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $g$ in $\exp(O(n e^{- g}))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$
  All four results follow from verifying the hypotheses of a new framework we call C-3PO. At a high level, the C-3PO algorithm proceeds by enumerating small cuts and reconstructing the original measure through cluster expansions. Underlying the algorithm is an improvement of subspace enumeration methods via active regression.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Closing All-Exp Gaps in Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximum Constraint Assignment
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove the all-exp property for the Traveling Salesman Problem with the $2$-opt neighborhood, and for $(3,2,2)$- and $(2,3,2)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment with the flip neighborhood. The all-exp property states that infinitely many instances have an initial solution from which every sequence of improving moves to a local optimum, and hence every run of local search, has exponential length. For the Traveling Salesman Problem, the all-exp property was previously known for every $k$-opt neighborhood with $k \ge 3$, so our result for $2$-opt completes the picture for all $k$-kopt neighborhoods. In $(p,q,r)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment, each constraint involves at most $p$ variables, each variable occurs in at most $q$ constraints, and each domain has size $r$. Decreasing any of the parameters of $(3,2,2)$ or $(2,3,2)$ yields a problem in which every sequence of improving flips has polynomial length, so both Maximum Constraint Assignment results are tight. All three results settle long-standing open problems. Our proofs build on a common construction idea, which reveals a close connection between the local-search dynamics of the three problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound.
  We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Revisiting the directed pathwidth of h-semicomplete digraphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A digraph is $h$-semicomplete if every vertex has at most $h$ non-neighbors. In semicomplete digraphs, $k$-triples are obstructions to bounded directed pathwidth with many algorithmic applications: Fradkin and Seymour [JCTB 2013] showed that a large triple contains a subdivision of every small digraph, and triples were used for irrelevant vertex arguments in routing problems by Fomin and Pilipczuk [JCTB 2019] and Gomes, Lopes, and Sau [ICALP 2025]. Fradkin and Seymour also showed that there is a function $f(k)$ such that every semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth at least $f(k)$ contains a $k$-triple, and their proof gives $f(k)$ triply exponential in $k$. For $h$-semicomplete digraphs, a result of Kitsunai et al. [ESA 2015] also yields a $k$-triple, but only existentially, and finding one in fixed-parameter time remained open. We improve the bound on $f(k)$ to a single exponential and extend the result to $h$-semicomplete digraphs: we show that every $h$-semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth greater than $(h+1) \cdot k \cdot 2^{27k+9}$ contains a $k$-triple, which we find in polynomial time, and no bound subexponential in $k$ or sublinear in $h$ is possible. We also extend the approximation algorithm for directed pathwidth of Fomin and Pilipczuk to $h$-semicomplete digraphs, so its certificates of large directed pathwidth remain valid. Our proof is much shorter than the analysis of Kitsunai et al., and while their algorithm is exact, ours runs in polynomial time. As an application, we show that Arc-Disjoint Paths on $h$-semicomplete digraphs is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by the number of paths and $h$, generalizing the semicomplete case. Finally, unlike in semicomplete digraphs, directed pathwidth does not bound directed cliquewidth: for every $k$, some acyclic $1$-semicomplete digraph, so of directed pathwidth zero, has directed cliquewidth at least $k$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Compressing the Lawler-Moore Dynamic Program for Weighted Tardy Jobs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The classic scheduling problem of minimizing the total weight of tardy jobs ($P_m||\sum_jw_jU_j$) asks for a schedule of jobs each with a processing time, weight, and due date on a constant number of parallel identical machines. A job is late in a schedule if it completes after its due date, and an optimal schedule is one where the total weight of all late jobs is minimized. The classic dynamic programming algorithm of Lawler and Moore [Manag. Sci., 1969] solves this problem in $O(nd_{\max}^m)$ where $n$ is the number of jobs, $d_{\max}$ is the maximum due date of any job, and $m$ is the number of identical machines. We show that it is sufficient to only compute part of the dynamic program and obtain the running time $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^{m + 1})$ where $\tilde{O}$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This affirmatively answers the open question posed by Hermelin, Molter, and Shabtay [INFORMS J. Comput., 2024], whether a running time of $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^2)$ is possible on a single machine.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Degree Realization with Maximum Matching
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Maximum Matching Degree Realization problem requires, for a sequence $d$ of $n$ positive integers, to compute a realizing graph(whose degree sequence corresponds to $d$) with the maximum possible matching. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. The decision version of this problem requires to determine whether a sequence $d$ admits a realization with a matching of size $ν$ (without computing such a realization). Recently, it was shown that it can be done by verifying a series of inequalities. We improve the existing characterization by reducing the number of inequalities.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Catalytic space-efficient algorithms for Distance and Determinant
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Catalytic computation reuses potentially large but in-use space (or catalytic space) which must be restored to its initial contents while the clean space is small. This allows all problems in $\mathsf{NL}$ and even larger classes to be in catalytic logspace [Buhrman et al, STOC2014]. In [Chmel et al, CCC2026] the catalytic space for reachability was restricted to sublinear space (specifically, $n \big/ 2^{θ(\sqrt{\log n})}$ space) while remaining in polynomial time. This matches the non-catalytic bounds from [Barnes et al, SICOMP1998].
  We extend the reachability bound to shortest distance, proving a simultaneous sublinear catalytic space and polynomial time bound (henceforth called, sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$). This is the first simultaneous sublinear space and polynomial time bound for distance even without the catalytic discipline. Moreover, our bound works even for polynomially weighted graphs.
  Along the way we prove simultaneous near linear catalytic space ($\mathcal{O}(n\log^{O(1)}{n})$) and polynomial time bounds for the determinant. We also show some applications to planar matching problems.
  Our starting point was catalytic computation of reachability in directed graphs by [Cook-Pyne, ITCS2026]. [Edenhofer, arXiv:2602.21088] used it to give a tradeoff between catalytic and non-catalytic space, while [Chmel et al, CCC2026] compress the graph to a smaller graph preserving $s,t$-reachability to achieve a smaller space bound. All three can be modified to yield an algorithm for unweighted distance.
  Our contribution is to define an approximation to the walk polynomial in weighted graphs that allows us to infer weighted $s,t$-distance in sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$. We do so by non-trivially combining elements from each of the above three papers.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Hypergraph Unreliability
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all-terminal unreliability in explicitly represented undirected hypergraphs of arbitrary rank. The algorithm estimates the probability that independent hyperedge failures disconnect the hypergraph, allowing a different rational failure probability for every edge. For a common failure probability, this improves the quasi-polynomial approximation schemes of Cen, Li, and Panigrahi to polynomial time and answers the polynomial-time approximation question reiterated in their subsequent work on graphs.
  The construction turns their representative-survival bound into an importance sampler whose relative second moment is bounded solely in terms of the number of vertices. We protect one randomly chosen representative pair during contraction, correct the path likelihood, and divide by the number of pairs surviving at the end. The resulting unbiased estimator has relative second moment at most $\binom n2$, even when unreliability is exponentially small.
  A minimum-cut normalization makes this estimator implementable with polynomially bounded precision: the residual likelihood becomes a survival probability in an auxiliary absorbing process, which admits rational discretization with a fixed random-bit budget. Logarithmic rate rounding and an exact weighted minimum cut extend the construction to unequal rational failure probabilities. The algorithm's worst-case running time and random-bit usage are polynomial in the input length, the inverse relative error, and $\log(1/δ)$ for confidence $1-δ$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Better Lower Bound for Sublinear Metric Steiner Tree
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the metric Steiner tree problem, we are given an $n$-point metric space $(V,w)$ and a set of terminals $T\subseteq V$, and we are interested in the smallest total weight $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ of a tree that contains every terminal and may also use points of $V\setminus T$. We work in the distance-oracle model: the algorithm knows $V$ and $T$ in advance and learns $w$ only by querying a single entry $w(u,v)$ at a time. The goal is to estimate $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ with the minimum number of queries.
  A factor of $2$ is achievable with nearly linear number of queries, so the interesting question is the query complexity of algorithms with an approximation ratio strictly below $2$. We prove that for every fixed $η\in(0,1)$, every randomized $(2-η)$-approximation algorithm must make more than $\widetildeΩ(n^{7/5})$ queries, improving upon the previously known bound of $\widetildeΩ(n^{6/5})$. Given that the best known upper bound shows that $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$ queries suffice, the exponent of this problem now lies between $7/5$ and $5/3$, up to logarithmic factors.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Lowered crossover points of Anthropic's subexponential 3-SAT algorithm
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The October 2026 refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis count satisfying assignments in time $2^{o(n)}$, but an asymptotic bound does not say from which input size, the crossover point, they beat the best known algorithms. We make the #3-SAT recursion of Anthropic's algorithm explicit and lower its crossover points, computed from the main term of the proved bound, by proved changes. For the bound in the number $m$ of clauses, at clause density one, the crossover point drops to about $2^{420}$ clauses from $2^{33858}$; for general 3-SAT, in the number $n$ of variables, our estimate drops to $2^{8.6\cdot10^9}$ variables from $2^{2.2\cdot10^{12}}$. With integer tables the recursion counts, for every $j$, the assignments satisfying exactly $j$ clauses in time $2^{O(m/\sqrt{\log m})}$. We observe that this refutes the Sparse Max-3-SAT Hypothesis of Alman and Vassilevska Williams, which also follows from either refutation by the reduction of Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, and we lower the crossover point of this computation to about $2^{1016}$ clauses from $2^{68364}$. The distance is structural: we define a rewrite-and-merge class that contains the recursion and all our constructions, and prove that in the main-term model no grid algorithm in it can gain for general 3-SAT below about $2^{6000}$ variables. For two balanced homogeneous merges we prove with quantum functionals an exponent of at least $(\log_2K)^{-3}$ per edge bit, which excludes running times $2^{n^{1-c}}$. Independently of SAT, we formalise the algorithm as a model of computation, Signed Network Sums, which contains rank-one methods and contraction trees. On the complete graph with four nodes, one-level constructions contract the network in $N^{23/6}$ if $ω=2$ and in about $N^{3.93}$ on the current (preprint) matrix-multiplication curve, below the bound $N^4$ of every rank-one method or contraction tree.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: List 3-Coloring in tame classes of graphs in quasipolynomial time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A class of graphs $\mathcal{G}$ is tame if there is a constant c such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ has at most $n^c$ minimal separators. Many important graph classes are tame, including chordal graphs, permutation graphs, and circle graphs. Several fundamental problems, most notably Max Weight Independent Set, can be solved in polynomial time on every tame class, which explains in a unified way their tractability on all these classes.
  We show that List 3-Coloring can be solved in quasipolynomial time on every tame class of graphs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Accelerated Approximate Optimization of Multi-Commodity Flows on Directed Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We provide $m^{1+o(1)}kε^{-1}$-time algorithms for computing multiplicative $(1 - ε)$-approximate solutions to multi-commodity flow problems with $k$-commodities on $m$-edge directed graphs, including concurrent multi-commodity flow and maximum multi-commodity flow.
  To obtain our results, we provide new optimization tools of potential independent interest. First, we provide an improved optimization method for solving $\ell_{q, p}$-regression problems to high accuracy. This method makes $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(k)$ queries to a high accuracy convex minimization oracle for an individual block, where $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(\cdot)$ hides factors depending only on $q$, $p$, or $\mathrm{poly}(\log m)$, improving upon the $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(k^2)$ bound of [Chen-Ye, ICALP 2024]. As a result, we obtain the first almost-linear time algorithm that solves $\ell_{q, p}$ flows on directed graphs to high accuracy. Second, we present optimization tools to reduce approximately solving composite $\ell_{1, \infty}$-regression problems to solving $m^{o(1)}ε^{-1}$ instances of composite $\ell_{q, p}$-regression problem. The method builds upon recent advances in solving box-simplex games [Jambulapati-Tian, NeurIPS 2023] and the area convex regularizer introduced in [Sherman, STOC 2017] to obtain faster rates for constrained versions of the problem. Carefully combining these techniques yields our directed multi-commodity flow algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Steiner Tree Parameterized by Multiway Cut: Single-Exponential Time and Polynomial Space
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the Steiner Tree problem, the goal is to find a minimum-weight tree containing a given set of terminals in an edge-weighted graph. Given a multiway cut of size $s$, we propose a deterministic algorithm running in $2^{O(s)}\operatorname{poly}(n,b)$ time and polynomial space ($n$ vertices, non-negative $b$-bit integer weights). A multiway cut for the terminals is a set of vertices whose deletion leaves at most one terminal in each connected component. This result answers a question of Jansen and Swennenhuis (ESA 2024). Building on their component decomposition, we show that it suffices to connect the selected cut vertices together with $O(s)$ additional terminals and attach the remaining terminals by shortest paths. We use colour coding to optimize over the choice of these additional terminals.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: New bounds for online coloring three-colorable graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We prove new lower and upper bounds for online coloring of three-colorable graphs, improving classical bounds of Vishwanathan [FOCS'1990] that have stood for more than three decades. For the lower bound against deterministic algorithms, we improve Vishwanathan's $Ω(\log^2n)$ to \(\exp\!\bigl(Ω((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})\bigr)\). For the upper bound of randomized algorithms, we give a randomized algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{n})$ improving Vishwanathan's $O(\sqrt{n \log n})$.
  Technically, for the lower bound construction, we introduce the language of $t$-fold coloring for simpler description of recursive construction, and the notion of post-degree for future control, and use the flexibility of two-sided colors of bipartite graph, constructed using the independent set amplification method of Vishwanathan, as building blocks to ensure three-colorability. The randomized algorithm integrates, in a new way, some of the ideas in offline coloring of Wigderson and Blum with ideas of Vishwanathan in the online setting, such as the degree control from Wigderson, the offline-monochromatic class from Blum, and the anchor-sampling from Vishwanathan and the CBIP algorithm by Lov{á}sz, Saks and Trotter.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Approximation Guarantees for Periodic-Review Stochastic Inventory Control
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In periodic-review stochastic inventory control, replenishment policies must balance holding and backlogging costs while responding to uncertain demands and evolving forecasts that may be arbitrarily correlated and nonstationary. In this general information setting, Levi, P{á}l, Roundy, and Shmoys (Mathematics of Operations Research 2007) established that the fully adaptive optimum can be approximated within factor $2$, which had remained the best-known performance guarantee since then. Their marginal cost accounting and dual-balancing framework made this comparison possible without computing optimal decisions across future trajectories, opening a broad research program on approximation algorithms for stochastic inventory systems.
  We break this long-standing barrier for periodic-review stochastic inventory control, showing how to compete against the fully adaptive benchmark within factor $\frac{ e }{ e-1 } \approx 1.582$ while retaining general demand correlations and evolving forecasts. We attain these advances by discovering a structural connection between marginal inventory accounting and weighted stopping problems, where each unit's conditional holding charge forms a supermartingale, while postponing its order incurs a history-dependent backlog charge. To leverage the random thresholding approach of Ma and Tzamos (ICML 2023) in this context, we develop a potential-function analysis, leading to an $\frac{ e }{ e-1 }$-approximation with respect to any unit's stopping problem. Subsequently, our common-threshold policy coordinates these marginal decisions into a global replenishment policy without additional loss.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Massively Parallel Algorithms for Huffman Coding
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Huffman coding is one of the oldest and most fundamental problems in computer science. Given a string of length $\TextLength$ over a general alphabet, the goal is to assign a binary codeword to each character so that no codeword is a prefix of another and the total encoded length of the string is minimized. Huffman coding is widely used in practical compression systems, including file compression. As modern datasets continue to grow, it is natural to study whether a Huffman code can be constructed efficiently in the massively parallel computation (\MPC) model. The celebrated Huffman coding algorithm admits two straightforward \MPC implementations: for any constant $ε\in(0,1)$, one uses $O(\TextLength^ε)$ memory per machine but requires $Θ(\log \TextLength)$ rounds, while the other runs in $O(1)$ rounds but requires $Θ(\sqrt{\TextLength})$ memory per machine. We give the first nontrivial \MPC algorithm for Huffman coding that bypasses both limitations. For every constant $ε>0$, our algorithm uses $O_ε(\log\log \TextLength)$ rounds and $\softO(\TextLength^ε)$ memory per machine, while its total memory and total computation are $\softO(\TextLength)$.
  {\color{black}Although our framework is tailored to the \MPC model, we show that it has applications in the \PRAM setting as well. Specifically, we show that the same algorithm can be implemented in the \PRAM model with total work close to linear. In particular, whenever the text length is at most $2^{O\left(\left(\frac{\log \AlphabetSize}{\log\log \AlphabetSize}\right)^2\right)}$ (slightly superpolynomial), where $\AlphabetSize$ is the alphabet size, our parallel running time is asymptotically better than that of all previously known \PRAM algorithms and is essentially optimal.}

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We propose the random-sign Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) for calibration-free self-sizing after decoding failure. In a two-round set
  reconciliation protocol, the receiver uses the failed first-round table to estimate an upper bound on the unknown difference size $d$ and size the
  second-round table. In standard IBLTs, failure selection couples the overlap bias with the sign composition of the set difference, making practical
  sizing depend on offline simulation calibration.
  A shared pseudorandom sign independent of the position mapping removes this dependence while preserving cell fields, field widths, and ideal peeling
  recovery. We prove exact unbiasedness on every fixed mapping, a Gaussian limit after failure for $d\gg\sqrt M$, and a discrete limit dominated by
  duplicate edge pairs at smaller scales, where $M$ is the number of cells. These results yield a Skellam upper-bound rule whose conditional miss rate
  is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all $d\ge2$, without offline calibration.
  More than 500 million paired decoding trials and end-to-end protocol experiments support the design. For small differences, the Gaussian rule's
  conditional miss rate exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8. The Skellam rule meets the target within sampling error across all 189 tested
  load configurations. Total two-round communication approaches that of an oracle using the true $d$ in the same protocol. With fixed deployment
  parameters, precomputed table lookup reduces sizing to less than one microsecond, with total protocol time within 0.5 percent of the Gaussian rule.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The implementation, frozen experimental configurations, and summary data are available at https://github.com/whitewum/random-sign-artifact

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Multiple Swap Local Search Approximations for Uniform-Cost Capacitated Facility Location with Extensions to Outliers
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities.
  Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments.
  It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Traveling Salesman Problem on Graphs with Proportional Independent Set
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a deterministic algorithm for minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in undirected graphs with arbitrary real edge costs and an independent set of size at least $αn$, for any fixed $3/7<α\le1/2$. It runs in $O^*(γ(α)^n)$ time for an explicit constant $γ(α)<2$; for bipartite graphs, the bound is $O^*((1+2\sqrt2)^{n/2})\approx O^*(1.957^n)$. The algorithm is based on a restricted Held--Karp dynamic program. Its state enumeration uses structural properties of minimum-cost assignments arising from a regular triangulation of a product of simplices.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Competitive Ratio of Online Budgeted Allocation is Strictly Smaller than $1-1/e$
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A well-known conjecture in online algorithms is that the (randomized) competitive ratio of online budgeted allocation is $1-1/e$. We refute this conjecture and show that every randomized online algorithm has competitive ratio at most $1 - 1/e - \varepsilon$ for a (small) absolute constant $\varepsilon > 0$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Stochastic Weighted Caching with Per-Request Predictions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Both the unweighted and weighted variants of caching are cornerstone problems in competitive analysis, with tight randomized competitive ratios of $Θ(\log k)$, where $k$ is the cache size. We study weighted caching with per-request predictions, where each page request is accompanied by a prediction of the next arrival time of the same page. For unweighted caching, such perfect predictions suffice to implement Belady's offline optimal rule. For weighted caching, however, previous work shows that a logarithmic lower bound persists even with perfect predictions on adversarial request sequences. Stochastic assumptions alone are also insufficient: the classical caching lower bounds already apply to uniform independent requests. In this work, we ask whether combining these two sources of additional information can overcome this barrier, and answer this question affirmatively.
  Specifically, we develop an efficient cache eviction policy that achieves a competitive ratio of $15.75$ using perfect per-request predictions when page requests are drawn independently from an arbitrary, known static distribution in every step, and page costs are arbitrary. Underlying our analysis is a novel lower bound on the optimal cost obtained through an ex-ante relaxation of the cache's covering constraints. Our algorithm's performance degrades gracefully under erroneous predictions: we prove a bound of $O(\min\{1+E,\log k\})$ on the competitive ratio, where $E$ aggregates each page's average prediction error, and may be unknown to the algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-δ$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible.
  Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study.
  Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries.
  We complement the upper bound with an $Ω(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Bandwidth vs BFS Width in Matrix Reordering, Graph Reconstruction, and Graph Drawing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We provide the first approximation quality guarantees for the Cuthull-McKee heuristic for reordering symmetric matrices to have low bandwidth, and we provide an algorithm for reconstructing bounded-bandwidth graphs from distance oracles with near-linear query complexity. To prove these results we introduce a new width parameter, BFS width, and we prove polylogarithmic upper and lower bounds on the BFS width of graphs of bounded bandwidth. Unlike other width parameters, such as bandwidth, pathwidth, and treewidth, BFS width can easily be computed in polynomial time. Bounded BFS width implies bounded bandwidth, pathwidth, and treewidth, which in turn imply fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for many problems that are NP-hard for general graphs. In addition to their applications to matrix ordering, we also provide applications of BFS width to graph reconstruction, to reconstruct graphs from distance queries, and graph drawing, to construct arc diagrams of small height.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of the paper published at ESA 2025

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Max Weight Independent Set in graphs with no long claws nor large induced bicliques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The complexity of Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw is one of the central open problems in algorithmic graph theory. We show that MWIS can be solved in polynomial time in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw and a fixed biclique as an induced subgraph. This strengthens a result of Abrishami, Chudnovsky, Dibek, Pilipczuk, and Rzążewski [ACM TALG 2026] who showed an analogous result, but under a stronger assumption that some biclique is excluded as a subgraph.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online carpooling against an oblivious adversary
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the online carpooling problem, edges on $n$ vertices arrive one at a time and must be oriented immediately, so as to keep the difference between the indegree and the outdegree of every vertex small. We give a randomized online algorithm which bounds the largest absolute difference over the first $T$ edges by $O((\log T)^{1/3})$ with high probability on every input sequence fixed in advance. This proves a conjecture of Kulkarni, Reis and Rothvoss and matches the known worst case lower bound. The algorithm keeps the law of the discrepancy vector dominated in the convex order by a Gaussian measure, and forces the endpoint with the smaller discrepancy to receive the edge whenever the two discrepancies are far apart. In the analysis we show that a vertex of discrepancy $D$ is preceded by a set of $O(D)$ vertices with total discrepancy $Ω(D^2)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Theoretical Analysis of Byte-Pair Encoding
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a widely used method for subword tokenization, with origins in grammar-based text compression. It is employed in a variety of language processing tasks such as machine translation or large language model (LLM) pretraining, to create a token dictionary of a prescribed size. Most evaluations of BPE to date are empirical, and the reasons for its good practical performance are not well understood.
  In this paper we focus on the optimization problem underlying BPE: finding a pair encoding that achieves optimal compression utility. We show that this problem is APX-complete, indicating that it is unlikely to admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme. This answers, in a stronger form, a question recently raised by Zouhar et al.
  On the positive side, we show that BPE approximates the compression utility of the optimal pair encoding to a worst-case factor between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.4324$. Our results aim to explain the ongoing success of BPE and are, to our knowledge, the first rigorous guarantees on its compression utility that hold for all inputs.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Extended version of ESA 2026 paper. Changes in v2: (1) an upper bound of ~0.4324 on the approximation ratio of BPE, improving the earlier 0.625, and (2) a modified proof of Claim 5, fixing an inaccuracy in v1

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Component-Weighted Centroid Search for Exact Incremental BPE
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Exact incremental tokenizers keep the tokenization of a growing text up to date, so a long prompt or agent trace is not retokenized each time it grows. Jiang and Gong's algorithm does this for byte-pair encoding (BPE) in $O(\log^2 t)$ worst-case time per byte, where $t$ is the length of the longest token. Its search passes through $O(\log t)$ nested subproblems and runs a binary search over the possible branches at each one. We weight each branch by the size of the subproblem it leads to. Each step then costs about one probe for every halving of the remaining candidates, and a whole update costs $O(\log t)$, as much as one binary search over all candidates. Output and asymptotic memory are unchanged. We also construct valid BPE vocabularies on which the original search provably needs $Θ(\log^2 t)$ probes and ours $Θ(\log t)$, and a Rust implementation reproduces both counts exactly. On six real vocabularies the two searches run at about the same speed on ordinary text, while on long runs of spaces or hyphens the weighted search is up to 2.5$\times$ faster.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: AXIOM: Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures, appendix

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: FastHeapDict: Permanent Slot Indexing for Efficient Decrease-Key Operations in Indexed Priority Queues
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Efficient decrease-key support remains an important practical concern in priority queues used by shortest-path and graph-processing algorithms. Although duplicate-entry heaps avoid explicit decrease-key operations and are simple to implement, they may accumulate many stale entries when tentative priorities are repeatedly improved. This paper presents FastHeapDict, an indexed binary min-heap based on permanent slot indexing. Instead of repeatedly locating keys through hash-table lookups during heap repair, FastHeapDict assigns each key a stable integer slot and stores that slot directly in heap entries. As a result, position updates during sift-up and sift-down operations are performed through integer indexing while preserving the usual indexed-heap interface. We evaluate FastHeapDict in both Python and C++20 using Dijkstra's algorithm as the primary experimental workload. The benchmarks include constructed dense stress graphs, randomized dense graph variants, and comparisons against duplicate-entry heaps and existing priority-queue alternatives. Across the tested Python workloads, FastHeapDict consistently outperforms the duplicate-entry heapq baseline and the tested heapdict and pqdict implementations. In the C++20 implementation, FastHeapDict also achieves strong constant-factor improvements over std::priority_queue duplicates, std::set-based decrease-key, and std::multiset duplicates. These results indicate that permanent slot indexing can provide a compact and effective implementation strategy for indexed priority queues in workloads where priority updates are frequent.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Preprint; Python and C++20 implementations. Source code and benchmark artifacts available at https://github.com/hojjatgoudarzi/FastHeapDict

Information Retrieval.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

Information Retrieval.title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding-model adaptation across domains and tasks
Information Retrieval.summary: AI agents require specialised retrieval across domains and tasks, but adapting embedding models is constrained by costly manual training-data design. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a self-improving agentic data synthesis framework that turns a few retrieval examples into reusable synthesis instructions. Given an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs, SYNTRA infers implicit information needs and relevance criteria, then uses feedback on trial outputs to refine instructions for query generation and relevance assessment. Experiments across 24 datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate that the same synthesis workflow produces effective training data, benefiting even strong embedding models with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement strengthens this supervision on all six evaluated tasks, yielding better retrieval than human calibration on four. The training value persists at larger scales: on MS MARCO, retrieval gains continue across a 32-fold range of synthetic training-data sizes. SYNTRA thus enables scalable embedding-model adaptation with minimal human intervention.
Information Retrieval.comment: 32 pages, 6 figures; supplementary information included (27 pages). Code: https://github.com/zucanlv/SYNTRA . Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZucanLyu/SYNTRA

Information Retrieval.title: TileMaxSim: Roofline Regimes and Compression Limits for Fused GPU MaxSim Scoring
Information Retrieval.summary: MaxSim scoring dominates the cost of multi-vector retrieval. Several groups built fused GPU kernels for it independently during 2026, and all report one measure of success: the fraction of peak memory bandwidth reached. That measure assumes the operator is limited by the bytes it moves.
