For locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, we preserve $O(\log^* n)$ complexity under any number of crashes whenever this bound holds without faults on all graphs with a fixed degree bound. In contrast, we construct an LCL on graphs of maximum degree at most five with fault-free complexity $Θ(\log n)$ and crash-tolerant complexity $Θ(n)$. Finally, any fault-free sinkless-orientation algorithm can be transformed to tolerate any number of crashes with only one additional round, guaranteeing correctness even at surviving nodes adjacent to crashes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: NP-Hardness and a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, with Applications to Dense Subgraphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Given intervals and points on a line, each point with a demand, and a budget $K$, Maximum Interval Multicover asks for at most $K$ intervals that satisfy as many points as possible, a point being satisfied if it lies in at least as many chosen intervals as its demand. One application is committee elections in which each candidate is approved by consecutive voters and voters have individual demands. Xu, Ran and Zhang introduced the problem and gave a $1/2$-approximation; the objective is not submodular when demands exceed one. Li, Tu, Zhang and Cao gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the minimization counterpart, unweighted partial interval multicover, and asked for its complexity. We prove that both problems are NP-hard, even for intervals of equal length; as their optima are integers bounded by the input size, neither has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We then give a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, also for arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing rewards for the coverage of each point. Building on a decomposition from Nonner's PTAS for Densest $k$-Subgraph on interval graphs, our scheme cuts the line into pieces at a small loss and solves every piece exactly. The key dynamic program handles intervals crossing a common point by choosing an interleaving of their left and right endpoints rather than sweeping along the line; it needs only two counters to track these intervals. The same algorithm yields PTASes on convex bipartite graphs for Bipartite Dense Subgraph, improving on the ratio $2/3$ of Backer and Keil for the subclass of bipartite permutation graphs, and on interval graphs for Maximum $k$-Vertex Cover and weighted clique counts.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-Majority, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-Majority achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $$\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-Majority that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact minimum Birkhoff decompositions of doubly stochastic matrices with finite precision
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The minimum Birkhoff decomposition problem asks for a representation of a doubly stochastic matrix as a convex combination of as few permutation matrices as possible. This NP-hard problem arises in the scheduling of switches in data centers and satellite systems, in random assignments in economics and in the statistics of rankings. We consider doubly stochastic matrices whose entries are given with a fixed number of decimal digits and look for exact decompositions whose weights have the same precision. We propose a parallel method with three parts. For matrices built from few permutation matrices, the first part reads the weights from the frequencies of the entries and places them on the matrix positions by a rule that, given the correct weights, never fixes a position wrongly. The second part computes lower bounds from pairs of rows or columns, which remain valid for real weights, and from certificates of a satisfiability solver. For matrices built from many permutation matrices, the third part runs a beam search over steps that each make at least one entry zero. On 375 test instances with up to 100 rows, the method proves optimality for 208 instances, and 197 of these proofs also hold for real weights. Of the 190 instances built from few permutation matrices, 187 are solved to proven optimality, 180 of them within one second. Compared with the best exact decompositions known before, the new decompositions are shorter for 278 instances and never longer.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximate Dual Separation for the Cluster LP: a 1.387-approximation for Correlation Clustering
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a $(1.3865+ε)$-approximation for correlation clustering on complete graphs, improving the previous best factor of $1.485+ε$ of Cao et al. (STOC'24).
  Our first main contribution is an efficient weak separation oracle for the cluster-LP dual. Given signed vertex weights $q$, it either finds a set $S$ with $q(S)>cost(S)$ or certifies that $q/(1+ε)$ is dual feasible, where $cost(S)$ measures the correlation clustering disagreements attributed to $S$ in any clustering in which $S$ is a cluster. Via the ellipsoid method, this yields $(1+ε)$-approximate primal and dual solutions for the fractional cluster LP in deterministic time $2^{poly(1/ε)}n^{O(1)}$ . The separator works directly on the original instance, without global preclustering: a novel localization argument restricts the search to a small universe, where weak regularity handles the resulting dense quadratic minimization. Complementing this result, we prove that exact dual separation and cluster-LP optimization are NP-hard, even for complete unweighted instances.
  Our second main contribution is a new rounding of the cluster LP. It combines cluster-based rounding with a continuous conditional pivot rule, and its analysis relies on single variance inequality with explicit weights. This bounds the cluster-LP integrality gap by $1.3865$, near its known lower bound of $4/3$, and gives a per-instance primal--dual certificate of approximation.
  Finally, we extend our separator to obtain a $(1.92+ε)$-approximation for seeded correlation clustering (where each cluster may contain at most one seed from a prescribed seed set), and to bounded-weight instances, yielding a deterministic polynomial-time approximate implementation of the cluster-insertion primitive used in combinatorial correlation clustering.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: revised organization to match conference submission

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Constructive FPT Algorithm for Integer Cone Optimization with Convex Costs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm for integer cone optimization with convex costs. Given $τ$ rational polytopes in $\R^{d+k}$, we combine generators whose first $d$ coordinates are integral and whose remaining $k$ coordinates may be fractional. Each generator has a convex cost depending only on its integer coordinates. We minimize the total cost of nonnegative integer combinations subject to arbitrary rational linear constraints on the full typewise aggregates and generator counts. Our algorithm runs in time \[
  2^{τ\log(τ+1)\,2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}, \] where $|I|$ is the total binary input length. It constructs an optimal representation using at most $2^{2d+1}$ distinct generators per type. The number $k$ of continuous coordinates contributes only to the polynomial input factor.
  For a single generator type, the running time becomes $2^{2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}$. Applications include constructive FPT algorithms for Cone and Polytope Intersection, high-multiplicity bin packing, vector bin packing, and makespan minimization on uniform and unrelated machines. The double-exponential dependence on $d$ is tight for Point-in-Cone and both bin-packing problems assuming $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}$. The mixed-integer formulation also yields additive EPTASs for makespan minimization, machine covering, and envy minimization on identical machines, and additive schemes fixed-parameter tractable in $1/\varepsilon+τ$ on uniform machines.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Faster Regular Expression Matching via Two-Dimensional Tabulation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Regular expression matching asks whether a string of length $n$ belongs to the language described by a regular expression of length $m$. We give an algorithm that solves this problem in linear space and $O(nm \log \log n/\log^2 n + n + m)$ time. This improves the leading term of the previous best worst-case constant-alphabet time bound by a factor of $\sqrt{\log n}$. The key new technique is a two-dimensional tabulation specialized to the regular expression.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Real-to-Integer Reduction for All-Pairs Shortest Paths
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Efficient graph algorithms often use techniques that are specific to integer-valued inputs and do not work for real-valued versions of the problems. Is it a limitation of current techniques, or are the real-valued variants inherently harder? One way to study this question is through real-to-integer reductions. We give (randomized, combinatorial) subcubic real-to-integer reductions for two central graph problems in fine-grained complexity: All-Pairs Shortest Paths and Exact Triangle. That is, we show that if the integer variants of these problems can be solved in truly subcubic time, then the real variants can also be solved in truly subcubic time.
  Our work extends and combines techniques from three previous works: (1) our real-to-integer reduction for the 3SUM problem (Fischer, Polak, Schmidt, FOCS 2026), which itself combines the Frank--Tardos theorem from optimization with Freiman's theorem from additive combinatorics; (2) universe reduction for APSP (Fischer, STOC 2026), which we generalize to reals and use to reduce the doubling of the set of edge weights; and (3) the ``Fredman's trick meets dominance product'' technique (Chan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, STOC 2023), which is needed to adapt the prior real-to-integer framework from equality constraints to inequalities.
  As a corollary, our reduction combined with Yuval's fast Integer APSP algorithm in the real RAM model with multiplication (IPL 1976) shows that the Real APSP Hypothesis is false in this model, which also follows from the very recent breakthrough by Alman and Vassilevska Williams using a very different approach.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Capacitated Clustering in Low Dimension with $(1+ε)k$ Centers
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In many applications of $k$-median and $k$-means, including load balancing and redistricting, each center can serve only a bounded number of clients. This leads to capacitated clustering, in which a client may be forced to use a distant center because all nearby ones are full. This loss of locality defeats the techniques behind approximation schemes, and no constant-factor approximation is known in general metrics even for capacitated $k$-median. A long line of work therefore opens $K=k+\lfloorεk\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $ε\in(0,1]$, while respecting the capacities exactly.
  We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for uniform soft capacities in low dimension, that is, when the clients or the center locations have bounded doubling dimension. With $K$ centers, its ratio is $3-2ε$ for $k$-median and $9-8ε$ for $k$-means, or $5-4ε$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Apart from $k$-median in the plane, these are the first polynomial-time ratios bounded by a constant independent of $ε$; previously, the best ratio was $O(ε^{-2}\log(1/ε))$, even for $k$-median. We also obtain ratios that stay bounded as $ε\to0$ for non-uniform and hard capacities in low dimension, and ratios polylogarithmic in $1/ε$ in general metrics.
  Our approach starts from a simple structural observation: a near-optimal uncapacitated solution can be split into fewer than $2k$ capacity-respecting blocks, so $2k$ centers already suffice, one per block. Our main tool, the rescue lemma, shows that once every block that sends clients to a center of the optimal solution is rescued (given a private center), that center can be closed, so each extra center effectively rescues about two blocks. This lets $\lfloorεk\rfloor$ extra centers rescue nearly an $ε$-fraction of the blocks, yielding the linear dependence on $ε$ in our ratios.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in a graph $G$ in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries that take as input variables the vertices $a$ and $b$ and are of the form ''are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between $a$ and $b$?''. All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. When starting from a biconnected graph, all updates take worst-case $O(\log n)$ time, and all queries are answered in $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get a deterministic algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case update and query time of $O(\log^2 n)$. Both algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Recovery Beats Storage: Improved Space for Preprocessed 3SUM
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The 3SUM problem asks, given sets $A,B,C$ of integers, whether there exist $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ whose sum belongs to $C$. In the preprocessed variant with unknown $C$, one preprocesses sets $A$ and $B$, each of size $n$, and subsequently answers a query specified by subsets $A'\subseteq A$, $B'\subseteq B$ and a target set $C'$ of size $O(n)$, by solving the 3SUM instance $(A',B',C')$. Kirkpatrick, Kuszmaul, Mathialagan, and Vassilevska Williams [ICALP 2026] gave the first algorithm with subquadratic space for this problem, achieving $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2+ε})$ query time using $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2ε/3})$ space, for every $ε\in[0,1/2]$. Their algorithm employs separate mechanisms for heavy and light targets, and for each heavy target it stores explicitly the list of pairs $(a,b)$ whose sum is congruent to it modulo a random prime $p$ but differs from it. These lists dominate the space bound. We present a unified construction that uses a single mechanism for all queries. Instead of storing these lists of pairs, our algorithm recovers on demand the residue class of the target modulo a random prime by inverting the function $(a,b)\mapsto (a+b\bmod p)$. Additionally, instead of storing the heavy targets, it recomputes at query time a set that covers them. This leads to an improved space bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-ε})$, while maintaining the same query time. Moreover, our construction is the first to achieve subquadratic space while supporting adaptively chosen queries.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Nearly optimal Personalized PageRank computation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the fundamental problem of computing Personalized PageRank (PPR) on an undirected and unweighted graph $G$. We focus on the $\eps$-error guarantee introduced by Andersen, Chung, and Lang [ACL; FOCS 2006 $\&$ Internet Math 2007]. Their classic local push method computes an approximate PPR vector satisfying the ACL $\eps$-error guarantee in $O((α\eps)^{-1})$ time, where $α$ is the teleportation parameter. This problem has a lower bound $Ω(\eps^{-1})$. Working with idealized SDDM solves, we eliminate the dependence on $α$ and present an algorithm that achieves the same error guarantee in $O(\eps^{-1-o(1)})$ time. Consequently, we obtain a nearly optimal algorithm for PPR computation under the ACL error guarantee, and a nearly linear algorithm for local graph clustering with complexity independent of $φ$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness.
  Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Learning Arbitrary Lindbladians from Time Evolution
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of learning arbitrary $n$-qubit Lindbladians, the generators of Markovian open-system dynamics, from their time evolution. We give the first known efficient algorithm that learns arbitrary Lindbladians without any structural assumptions. For an $n$-qubit Lindbladian of dynamical strength at most $Λ$, the algorithm estimates every coefficient to error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(Λ^2/\varepsilon^2)$ experiments and $\widetilde O(Λ/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, with classical running time polynomial in $n$ and $Λ/\varepsilon$. Both experimental costs match known lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The algorithm identifies candidate labels through product Pauli experiments and estimates their coefficients using random stabilizer preparations and Clifford measurements. It requires no ancillas or control during the unknown evolution.
  For constant $k$, our algorithm learns generic $k$-local Lindbladians of local dynamical strength at most $Λ_{\mathrm{loc}}$ using $\widetilde O(n^2Λ_{\mathrm{loc}}^2/\varepsilon^2)$ experiments and $\widetilde O(nΛ_{\mathrm{loc}}/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, improving the upper bounds of prior works in terms of the dependence on $n$. We further improve the lower bounds of Arad, Chen, Guo, Rebentrost, and Yu (SODA 2027) using a family of $3$-local Lindbladians. They already hold when the support is known, and only one Hamiltonian coefficient is requested, even for adaptive protocols with arbitrary ancillas and quantum memory. These lower bounds establish that our algorithm is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors in both experiment count and total evolution time for every fixed $k \geq 3$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 57 pages; lower bounds added in v2

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Scalable Exact Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering via Sparse Geographic Distance Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Exact hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) of large spatial datasets is limited in practice by the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and memory required for the full pairwise distance matrix. We present GSHAC (Geographically Sparse Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering), a system that makes exact HAC feasible at scales of millions of geographic features on a commodity workstation. GSHAC replaces the distance matrix with a sparse geographic distance graph containing only pairs within a user-specified geodesic bound $h_{\max}$, constructed in $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot k)$ time via spatial indexing, where $k$ is the mean number of neighbors within $h_{\max}$. Connected components of this graph define independent subproblems, and we prove that the resulting assignments are exact for all standard linkage methods at any cut height $h \le h_{\max}$. For single linkage, an MST-based path keeps memory at $\mathcal{O}(n_k + m_k)$ per component. Applied to a global mining inventory ($n = 261{,}073$), the system completes in 12 s (109 MiB peak HAC memory) versus $\approx 545$ GiB for the dense baseline. On a 2-million-point GeoNames sample, all tested thresholds completed in under 3 minutes with peak memory under 3 GiB. We provide a scikit-learn-compatible implementation for direct integration into GIS workflows.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for $(k,z)$-Clustering in Euclidean and Doubling Metrics
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We determine the optimal worst-case size of strong coresets for $(k,z)$-clustering in Euclidean spaces and doubling metrics, up to polylogarithmic factors.
  In Euclidean space, previous lower bounds matched the best upper bounds only for $\varepsilon\gtrsim k^{-1/(z+2)}$. We close the gap for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal size $\widetildeΘ(\min\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\})$ for every fixed $z\ge1$, all $k\ge1$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our lower bound replaces each offset in a previous hard instance by a group of distinct offsets. A fixed family of $k$-center queries and four-wise independent signs force a large relative cost error for every sufficiently small subset with arbitrary nonnegative weights.
  For doubling metrics of dimension $D$, we resolve the previously unmatched bounds for $z>2$. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde O(k^{2-2/z}D\varepsilon^{-2})$ and a lower bound that, together with known upper bounds, establishes the optimal size $\widetildeΘ(kD\min\{k^{1-2/z}\varepsilon^{-2},\,\varepsilon^{-z}\})$ for fixed $z>2$, $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_z$, and $D\ge C_z\log(2/\varepsilon)$, where $C_z>0$ and $\varepsilon_z\in(0,1)$ depend only on $z$. The lower bound exploits the ability to encode $Θ(D)$ independent signs per center without diluting relative cost discrepancy. For the upper bound, we use independent, unbiased two-point summaries that exactly preserve cluster mass and anchor cost, combined with iterative size reduction.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Bounds for $(1+ε)$-Approximation for Minimum Spanning Trees in Doubling Metrics
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The minimum spanning tree (MST) problem is one of the most basic optimization problems on metric spaces and graphs. We study the problem of computing a $(1+ε)$-approximation to the MST of an $n$-point metric space of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}$. In doubling metrics, previous deterministic algorithms incur a running time with dependence $ε^{-O(\mathrm{ddim})}$.
  We give a deterministic algorithm that computes a $(1+ε)$-approximate MST in time $$ O_{\mathrm{ddim}}\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}ε\log(1/ε)\right\}\right) $$ in the standard real RAM model with a unit-cost exact-distance oracle. For bounded doubling dimension, this improves the previous dependence on $ε$ to essentially linear in $ε^{-1}$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound of $$ Ω\!\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}ε\log(1/ε)\right\}\right) $$ on running time in the same model, already for metrics of doubling dimension at most seven, showing that our running time is essentially tight.
  For points in $\mathbb R^d$ with $d = O(1)$, exploiting Euclidean geometry allows us to further improve the dependence on $ε$. We obtain a $(1+ε)$-approximate MST in expected time $$ O_d\left( n \log n + \min\left\{n^2, \frac{n}{ε^{1 - β_d}} \log^{1-β_d}(1/ε) \right\} \right) $$ for some $β_d=Θ(1/d)$, improving the accuracy-dependent term $nε^{-2}\log^2(1/ε)$ of Arya and Mount [SODA'16].
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Improved running time for MST in doubling metrics, new upper bound for MST in Euclidean spaces, and lower bounds for MST in doubling metrics

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Learning Fourier-Sparse Signals and Multiband Signals
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A classical problem in continuous sparse Fourier transforms, which dates back to Prony's work in 1795, is to learn a $k$-Fourier-sparse signal $x(t):=\sum_{j=1}^k α_j e^{2 π\mathbf{i} f_j t}$ with arbitrary $k$ frequencies $f_1,\ldots,f_k \in \mathbb{R}$. We consider this learning problem within a fixed time window $t \in [-1,1]$ in the presence of bounded $L_2$ adversarial noise. Because the frequencies $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ can be arbitrarily close, accurately recovering individual frequencies is information-theoretically impossible even under exponentially small noise from Moitra (STOC 2015). This work therefore examines two fundamental questions: If an algorithm uses $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies to approximate $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ of $x$, what is the optimal covering error? And how can we efficiently learn the continuous signal $x(t)$ as a whole over the time window?
  Our main result is an algorithm running in time $\tilde{O}(k)$ that outputs a list $L$ of $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies with covering error $O(k)$ --- meaning that for most frequencies $f_j$ of $x$, $L$ guarantees $\min_{\tilde{f} \in L} |f_j-\tilde{f}| = O(k)$ --- and an reconstruction $\tilde{x}(t) \approx x(t)$ over $[-1,1]$. When constrained to outputting $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies, this $O(k)$ covering error is nearly optimal: Chen and Price (ICALP 2019) demonstrated two indistinguishable $k$-Fourier-sparse signals separated by distance $\tildeΩ(k^2)$ in the frequency domain, which implies an amortized lower bound of $\tildeΩ(k)$ per frequency. Furthermore, our sample and time complexities are nearly optimal, dramatically improving upon the previous best algorithm by Song, Sun, Weinstein, and Zhang (FOCS 2023), which required $\tilde{O}(k^4)$ samples and $\tilde{O}(k^{4ω})$ running time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Polynomial Kernel for Planar Directed Feedback Vertex Set
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Directed Feedback Vertex Set problem (DFVS) asks whether a digraph can be made acyclic by deleting at most $k$ vertices. Whether DFVS admits a polynomial kernel parameterized by $k$ is a major open problem in kernelization, even for planar digraphs. We resolve the planar case by giving a deterministic kernel with $O(k^{66}\log^2 k)$ vertices and arcs. Our algorithm proceeds in three stages. First, we apply structural reduction rules to the input digraph, bounding the number of directed faces and some special vertices. Second, we pass to the planar dual, where vertex deletion corresponds to adding groups of reverse arcs to make each weakly connected component strongly connected. The structural bounds in the first stage yield a small retained vertex set in the dual. We then compress the dual instance by identifying vertices with the same distance records from this retained vertex set. The main technical contribution is a directed-cut argument showing that this identification preserves feasibility. Finally, we transform the polynomial-size dual instance back into an instance of Planar Directed Feedback Vertex Set via a $3$-CNF encoding and a planar graph construction.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-linear-Time Sampling of the Ferromagnetic Ising Model at the Tree Uniqueness Threshold
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a near-linear-time sampler for the zero-field ferromagnetic Ising model throughout the tree-uniqueness regime, including the threshold itself. The method also gives sampling algorithms for the XY and integer Potts models. On an $n$-vertex graph with $m$ edges and maximum degree at most $Δ$, we obtain the following expected-work bounds, with total variation error at most $\varepsilon$.
  1.Near-linear Ising sampling. For $Δ\ge3$, the work is $O(n+m\log^3(n/\varepsilon))$ throughout the tree-uniqueness regime, including the threshold $β=Δ/(Δ-2)$.
  2.Almost-linear XY sampling. For $Δ\ge8$, we sample the XY model in $\widetilde O(m+n^{1+o(1)})$ expected work at inverse-polynomial accuracy up to and including the robust phase-transition threshold on the $Δ$-regular tree.
  3.Near-linear Potts sampling. For integer $q\ge3$, we sample the $q$-state Potts model in $\widetilde O(n+q^{O(1)}m)$ expected work whenever $β-1\le 0.1(β_{\mathrm{od}}(q,Δ)-1)$, where $β_{\mathrm{od}}$ is the ordered/disordered coexistence parameter.
  We express the even-subgraph representation of critical Ising as a polymer model that admits near-linear-time sampling, thereby bypassing the critical slowdown of Glauber and Swendsen--Wang dynamics. Building on the low-degree approximation approach of Miao and Yin, we establish general spectral conditions for fast polymer sampling. We verify these conditions through explorations that also implement the sampler efficiently, and apply the same framework to flow representations of the XY and Potts models. We also establish polynomial-time counting and sampling for the ferromagnetic XY model at every fixed temperature.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Vector Balancing in Polynomial Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Komlós problem asks for signs $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n$ with $\|A\varepsilon\|_\infty$ bounded by an absolute constant whenever the columns of $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ have Euclidean norm at most $1$. We give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem in the unit-cost real-RAM model. Our deterministic algorithm achieves discrepancy at most $8272$. As a consequence, we obtain a deterministic $O(\sqrt t)$-discrepancy algorithm for the Beck-Fiala problem on set systems in which each element belongs to at most $t$ sets.
  Our algorithm rounds a fractional coloring while keeping the row sums bounded. Its key idea is to keep the number of nearly tight row constraints small relative to the number of active coordinates. We achieve this through a spectral bound based on a weighted Gram matrix of squared row entries. We maintain the bound using a cubic spectral potential and negative-curvature updates that satisfy the required linear constraints.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Approximation for Constrained Correlation Clustering via Repulsion
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The best-known approximation factor for constrained correlation clustering stood at three for nearly two decades, until a recent improvement to below $16/7$. We give a randomized polynomial-time $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation using \emph{Repulsion}, a recursive operation that separates a metric ball from its complement. Repulsion naturally respects hard constraints and admits a short potential-based analysis; as a warm-up, radius-$2/3$ Repulsion rounds the standard metric LP into a feasible partition of cost at most three times its objective.
  The $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation takes a two-stage approach, first removing must-links with arbitrarily small loss in the approximation ratio. The second stage combines lossless, constraint-aware preclustering with the bounded sub-cluster LP framework of Cao, Cohen-Addad, Lee, Li, Newman, and Vogl (STOC 2024). Repeated positive conditioning and sampling produce candidate sets, which radius-one Repulsion partitions into feasible clusters at controlled cost.
  We also give an approximation-preserving reduction from vertex cover to cluster deletion, a special case with only cannot-links. Apart from establishing a matching factor-two hardness threshold under the Unique Games Conjecture, it motivates our two-stage approach and Repulsion.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximation Algorithms for Directed Telephone Multicast
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Telephone multicast is a classical problem in information dissemination. In the directed setting, a message starts at a source in an $n$-vertex digraph, and each informed vertex may call one out-neighbour per round. The goal is to inform a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. Despite previous work on telephone multicast, a substantial approximation gap remained in the directed setting: approximating the problem within a factor of $o(\log k)$ is NP-hard, while the best existing polynomial-time approximation guarantee depending only on $k$ was $\widetilde O(\sqrt{k})$.
  For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm that runs in $n^{O(\ell)}$ time and returns a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)(OPT+k^{1/\ell})$, where $OPT$ is the optimum number of rounds. This yields an $O(k^ε)$ approximation in time $n^{O(1/ε)}$ for every fixed $ε>0$, and an $O(\log^4 k)$ approximation in quasi-polynomial time. The same algorithm gives an $O(\log k)$ approximation whenever $OPT\ge k^ε$ for a fixed $ε\in(0,1)$, which is optimal up to a constant factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.
  On planar digraphs, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 k)$ approximation. More generally, we give an $O(p\log^2 k)$ approximation for minor-closed graph classes with the following separator property. Given any rooted spanning tree, a balanced separator can be computed in polynomial time as the union of all vertices on at most $p$ tree paths from the root to chosen vertices. Classes of bounded treewidth satisfy this property.
  We also strengthen the known logarithmic approximation hardness for directed telephone multicast, extending it from instances with a polynomially large optimum to instances with $OPT=O(\log k)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Nearly Optimal Submodular Sparsification, with and without Cardinality Constraints
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the sparsification of decomposable submodular functions: given a sum $F(S) = \sum_{i=1}^m f_i(S)$ of $m$ nonnegative submodular functions on an $n$-element ground set $[n]$ (without assuming monotonicity or symmetry), the goal is to find a sparse reweighting $\widetilde{F}(S) = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i f_i(S)$ with at most $s \ll m$ nonzero weights that preserves $F(S)$ within a $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$ factor across a target family of queries. For all subset queries $S \subseteq [n]$, we give a polynomial-time randomized algorithm that constructs a sparsifier of size $O(n^2 \log n / \varepsilon^2)$. This improves upon the previous best upper bound of $O(n^3 / \varepsilon^2)$ by Kenneth and Krauthgamer and resolves their open conjecture up to a logarithmic factor, matching the $Ω(n^2)$ lower bound from directed cuts. Motivated by capacity budgets in submodular applications and the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) in compressed sensing, we further study submodular sparsification under a cardinality constraint $|S| \le k$, and obtain a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs a sparsifier of size $O(n k \log n / \varepsilon^2)$, nearly matching the $Ω(nk)$ lower bound. This shows that a cardinality constraint unconditionally reduces the size of general submodular sparsifiers by a factor of roughly $k/n$; we complement this with $Ω(n)$ lower bounds showing that even regular symmetric or almost-regular monotone submodular functions cannot be sparsified to $o(n)$ size for $k = 2$ and $k = 1$, respectively.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Differentially Oblivious Priority Queues with Sublogarithmic Cost
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this paper, we study exact online integer priority queues under differential obliviousness in the balls-and-bins model. Given a public upper bound $T$ on the number of operations and assuming that the priorities are bounded by a polynomial in $T$, we construct an $(\eps,δ)$-differentially oblivious priority queue supporting insertion and minimum extraction, which requires $\polylog(T)$ private memory. For constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $δ=\exp(-Θ(\log^2 T))$, our construction incurs $O(\log T/\log\log T)$ expected amortized total work per operation, which breaks the $Ω(\log T)$ barrier for fully oblivious priority queues~[Jacob et al., SODA'2019]. Further, we prove a matching lower bound for $(\eps,δ)$-differentially oblivious priority queues with $\varepsilon=O(1)$ and $δ=o(1)$, which indicates that our construction is asymptotically optimal in terms of total work.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Testing for a Large Induced Expander: Sublinear Algorithms and Query Lower Bounds
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Testing expansion asks to distinguish graphs of large conductance from graphs that are far from having large conductance. We study a relaxation in which only part of the graph is required to expand: does an $n$-vertex graph of bounded degree contain an induced expander on a constant fraction of its vertices, when the rest of the graph, including the edges leaving the expander, is arbitrary? Let $P_{α,φ}$ denote the property of containing an induced subgraph on at least $αn$ vertices with inner conductance at least $φ$.
  For every constant $κ\in(0,1)$, we give a tester that accepts graphs in $P_{α,φ}$ and rejects graphs outside $P_{κα,μφ^2}$, where $μ=Θ_{α,κ}(1/\log n)$, using $O_{α,κ}(\sqrt n\,φ^{-2}\log n)$ queries. For fixed $α\in(0,1]$, $κ\in(0,1)$, and $0<φ\le9/20$, we further show that distinguishing these two classes requires $Ω_{α,κ,φ}(n^{1/2+c_{κ,φ}μ})$ queries for every sufficiently large $n$ and every $0<μ\le1$, where $c_{κ,φ}>0$. The bound holds for adaptive algorithms, uniformly in $μ$. Hence, for testers with $\sqrt n\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ queries, the logarithmic loss in conductance is necessary up to a $\log\log n$ factor. The same tester also permits distance-based rejection at a weaker conductance while retaining the original core size.
  Our tester compares the endpoint distributions of random walks from different vertices with each other, rather than with the uniform distribution. Its analysis uses the trace chain, which observes the walk only at its visits to the unknown expanding core. Our lower bound builds on the noisy-parity construction of [CKK+18], using vector-valued parity labels in $\mathbb F_2^r$ to create many hidden classes, each too small to contain a qualifying induced expander.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Near-Linear Element-Kernel for \(d\)-Hitting Set
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In \(d\)-Hitting Set, the input consists of a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\) of subsets of \(U\) with size at most \(d\), and an integer \(k\). The task is to decide whether at most \(k\) elements of \(U\) can intersect every set in \(\mathcal S\). Previously known kernels contain \(O(k^{d-1})\) elements and \(O(k^d)\) sets. Whether the number of elements can be reduced to \(O(k^{d-1-\varepsilon})\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) is a longstanding open problem in kernelization. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by giving a near-linear randomized element-kernel and a subquadratic deterministic element-kernel through a re-encoding of the instance. For every fixed \(d\geq3\), we give a one-sided randomized kernel with \(O_d(k\log^3k)\) elements and a deterministic kernel with \(O_d(k^{7/4}\log^{3/2}k)\) elements. Our kernels may still contain \(k^{O(d)}\) sets and the parameter \(k\) may grow polynomially.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $β=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$α< α_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings.
  Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms.
  As a key intermediate step, we establish the pointwise equivalence, away from the threshold, of three notions of replica symmetry: geometric (averaged pairwise correlation decay), thermodynamic (convergence to the Bethe free-energy prediction), and variational (nonpositivity of the Bethe functional).
  To establish zero-freeness, we develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, lifting classical small subgraph conditioning to random holomorphic functions to control short-cycle fluctuations. We also use variational replica symmetry to obtain exponential planted overlap concentration. This enables a typical-graph truncation that controls complex second moments up to the replica symmetry breaking threshold.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Revised and expanded: strengthened the characterization of the replica-symmetric phase, reorganized and expanded the proofs. 84 pages

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal (Randomized) Compact Routing Schemes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Compact routing schemes route messages along short paths while every vertex stores little information. We study the trade-off between the stretch and the storage of compact routing schemes in undirected graphs, in four models: labeled and name-independent schemes, with average or worst-case local storage. We improve the best known stretch in all four models.
  Our main result is a labeled routing scheme with expected stretch $2k-1$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ average local storage, in which only the routing is randomized. Under the Erdős girth conjecture, no scheme with this storage has stretch below $2k-1$, so our scheme is optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors in the storage. With deterministic routing, we obtain stretch $\approx2.47k$, the best known deterministic stretch with average storage.
  Worst-case local storage is the classical setting of compact routing. The leading coefficient $4$ in the stretch $4k-5$ of Thorup and Zwick~[SPAA'01] was improved only by Chechik~[PODC'13], to $\approx3.68$ in unweighted graphs. In unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(\frac83k+O(1),O(k))$, and deterministic stretch $\approx3.05k$.
  Name-independent routing is harder, since the source knows only the name of the destination. The best known stretch with $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ local storage in unweighted graphs was $96k$, by Abraham, Gavoille, and Malkhi~[DISC'04]. We improve it by more than a factor of $8$. With average storage, we obtain expected stretch $4k-5$, which matches the labeled scheme of Thorup and Zwick. With worst-case storage in unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(8k+O(1),O(k))$.
  All our schemes for unweighted graphs extend to weighted graphs with a small loss in the stretch, and still improve the previous unweighted bounds.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Criteria Network Design Problems
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Min-max multi-criteria optimization asks for a single feasible solution minimizing the maximum of its costs under $\ell$ nonnegative cost functions, a formulation that captures both fairness across groups and robustness across scenarios. It has proved hard to approximate even for basic problems: for robust shortest paths, polylogarithmic approximations are known only in quasi-polynomial time. For network design, the best known guarantee is an $\ell$-approximation, which is tight for the natural LP relaxation.
  We show that exponentially better and nearly optimal guarantees are achievable for two fundamental network design problems. For multi-criteria connectivity augmentation (MC-CAP), which asks to increase the edge connectivity of a given undirected graph by one, we give a randomized polynomial-time $O(\log \ell)$-approximation algorithm. Applying our augmentation procedure iteratively and analyzing its randomized choices jointly across iterations yields an $O(\log k \log \ell)$-approximation for the multi-criteria $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph (MC-$k$-ECSS) problem, for every $k \geq 2$. We complement these algorithms with a nearly matching lower bound: for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, MC-CAP admits no polynomial-time $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} \ell)$-approximation, even when the underlying graph is a star, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}\bigl(n^{\log^{O(1)}n}\bigr)$. The same hardness extends to the MC-$k$-ECSS problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Smallest Multiplicative Stretch for an $α$-APASP Below $\widetilde O \left(n^ω\right)$ Runtime
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Dor, Halperin and Zwick [FOCS'96; SICOMP'00] showed that $(2-\varepsilon)$-APASP is at least as hard as BMM for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$. Zwick [FOCS'98; JACM'02] gave a $2$-APASP algorithm in $\widetilde O(n^{ω+o(1)}\log W_{\max})$ runtime, where $W_{\max}$ is the maximum edge weight. Bringmann, K{ü}nnemann and W{ę}grzycki [STOC'19] removed this logarithmic factor. Using OpenAI's recent bound $ω\leq\frac{9}{4}$ gives $\widetilde O\left(n^{\frac{9}{4}+o(1)}\right)$ time.
  We present two weighted undirected $2$-APASP algorithms. The first uses $(\min,\max)$-products. Earlier rectangular FMM bounds of Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'24] and Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'25] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.36999465})$ runtime, below the previous $ω\leq2.371177$ of Dupont, Eisenberger, Kozlovskii, Mehrabian, Ruiz, See, Zhou, Alman, Vassilevska Williams and Balog [arXiv'26]. Current rectangular FMM bounds give $\widetilde O(n^{2.34549151})$, independent of $W_{\max}$.
  For integer weights, our second algorithm has $\widetilde O(n^{ω-\frac{(ω-2)^2}{ω-1}+o(1)}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$ runtime, with exponent below $ω$ whenever $ω>2$. The rectangular bounds of Uzna{ń}ski [arXiv'26] or of Amanov, van den Berg and Zuiddam [arXiv'26] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.17157288}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tree Covers for Directed Graphs: Distance Oracles, Routing Schemes and Spanners
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In a seminal work [STOC'01; JACM'05], Thorup and Zwick showed that every weighted undirected graph admits a tree cover where each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ trees in expectation, and every pair has a path of stretch at most $2k-1$ in some tree.
  In this paper, we extend this structural property to directed graphs with nonnegative edge weights. Let $\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v) = \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + \mathrm{dist}_G(v \to u)$ denote the roundtrip distance. For every integer $k$, we construct a collection $\mathcal{T}$ of tree-pairs, each consisting of an in-tree and an out-tree rooted at the same vertex. Each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ tree-pairs in expectation, and for every ordered pair $(u, v)$ some tree-pair $T_{in}\cup T_{out} \in \mathcal{T}$ satisfies $\mathrm{dist}_{T_{in}\cup T_{out}}(u \to v) \le \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + (k-1)\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v).$
  We call this a \emph{$k$-strong (roundtrip) tree cover}. While prior techniques partition distances into geometric scales and build separate structures for each scale, our construction handles all distances simultaneously within a single, unified hierarchy. This yields the first directed tree cover for general $k$ matching the classic Thorup-Zwick stretch-size trade-off. Our cover immediately implies improved constructions of roundtrip spanners, path-reporting distance oracles, and compact routing schemes, as well as their source-wise and prioritized variants. We also provide faster algorithms for these structures: for general $k \ge 4$, all the above objects can be constructed in $\widetilde{O}(\min\{mn, n^{2.5}\})$ expected time, breaking the $mn$ barrier in dense directed graphs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Finding Integer Roots of Polynomials in Nearly Optimal Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients of absolute value less than $2^b$. Using Pan's approximate factorization theorem, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds all distinct integer roots of $f$ in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations. This matches the bit size of the input up to logarithmic factors and does not require $f$ to be square-free. Since we were unable to verify parts of the running time analysis of Pan's theorem, we also give a self-contained deterministic algorithm with running time $\widetilde O(nb+\min(n,b)^3b^2)$, which is $\widetilde O(nb)$ whenever $b\leq n^{1/4}$. This answers a question of Harvey and Hittmeir (2022), who asked whether integer roots can be found deterministically in quasilinear time, conditionally on Pan's theorem, and unconditionally for $b\leq n^{1/4}$. The fastest previous deterministic algorithm, due to Nir, takes $\widetilde O(n^{3/2}b)$ bit operations and works only for square-free polynomials.
  Instead of $p$-adic lifting, we combine approximate complex root finding with exact polynomial evaluation. We first approximate the complex roots of the polynomial formed by the top $\min(n,b)+1$ coefficients of $f$. Every integer root $r$ of $f$ with $|r|\geq 2$ lies within distance $2$ of some complex root of this truncated polynomial. Rounding the real parts of the approximate roots therefore gives a list of $O(\min(n,b))$ candidate integers that is guaranteed to contain all integer roots of $f$. Although a single candidate can have up to $b$ bits, a bound via the Mahler measure shows that the bit lengths of all candidates sum to $O(b)$. This allows us to test all candidates by exact multipoint evaluation in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Pure Differentially Private Query Release via Laplace Input Smoothing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the offline release of a public family of $k$ statistical queries on a database of $N$ records from a public universe of size $d$, under pure $\varepsilon$-differential privacy. We give an efficient algorithm that, with probability at least $1-β$, answers all queries simultaneously to error
  $$O\left(\min\left\{1,\sqrt{\frac{\log(d/β)\log k}{N\varepsilon}}\right\}\right).$$ The output is a synthetic histogram on the data universe, and its running time depends polynomially on $N,d$ and $k$.
  This resolves a conjecture of Nikolov and Ullman (2021) with an efficient, polynomial-time construction. Fitzsimons (2026) recently established the same square-root error scale via an information-theoretic construction that relies on a computationally intractable Lipschitz envelope over the exponential space of possible outputs. In contrast, we introduce an input-side smoothing approach: we run a selection-only multiplicative-weights process after a single sparse Laplace perturbation of the input histogram. Departing from standard first-order stability analyses, we investigate the stability of stability by establishing a uniform lower bound on the second-order log-derivatives of the output transcript across $T$ rounds of multiplicative weight updates. We then develop an analytic smoothing principle showing that this curvature bound allows a sparse, coordinate-wise perturbation to guarantee pure differential privacy globally, attaining optimal utility through a conceptually simple, polynomial-time pure-DP mechanism.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Counting Linear Extensions Faster than $2^n$
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic algorithm that counts the linear extensions of any $n$-element poset in $O^*(33^{n/6}) \le O^*(1.791^n)$ time and space, breaking the $O^*(2^n)$ barrier of standard order-ideal dynamic programming without assumptions on height, width, or dimension.
  Our algorithm fixes an antichain $B$ and tracks order ideals only on the remaining core $V \setminus B$. For each element $v \in B$ that has successors in the core, we guess which of those successors appears first in the linear extension, reducing all upper constraints on $v$ to a single deadline. An element $v \in B$ becomes available once all of its core predecessors have been placed; available elements with the same deadline then face identical remaining constraints, so the dynamic program only needs to record how many available elements have each deadline and weight transitions by the number of choices for the next element.
  Taking $B$ to be a maximum antichain and balancing this dynamic program against a Dilworth chain partition yields an $O^*(1.89^n)$ algorithm. To obtain our main bound, we use a minimum-cut computation in an auxiliary bipartite network to find an antichain $B$ whose comparability neighborhood $R$ satisfies $|B| \ge 5|R|$ while the remainder $V \setminus (B \cup R)$ partitions into stars with at most five leaves. Since a $j$-leaf star has $2^j+1$ independent sets and $(2^j+1)^{1/(j+1)} \le 33^{1/6}$ for $1 \le j \le 5$, combining the star bound on the remainder with our state bound on $B \cup R$ gives $O^*(33^{n/6})$ time and space.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Max Independent Set Remains NP-hard when Excluding a Planar Induced Minor (and More)
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We show that Max Independent Set (MIS) remains NP-hard in graphs excluding the $5 \times 5$ grid as an induced minor. This negatively answers a question of Dallard--Milanič--Štorgel that has attracted sustained attention, and refutes a conjecture by Gartland and Lokshtanov.
  Unless $N$-variable 3-SAT can be solved in time $2^{\mathcal O(N^{1-\varepsilon})}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, MIS requires $2^{Ω(n^{1/2-o(1)})}$ time on $n$-vertex graphs in this class. This complements a $2^{\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})}$-time algorithm on any $H$-induced-minor-free class by Korhonen and Lokshtanov. Exploiting a connection between low twin-width or reduced parameters on one hand and planar-induced-minor-freeness on the other, we further show that 3-Coloring, Feedback Vertex Set and Dominating Set are NP-complete on weakly sparse graphs of reduced component max-leaf (hence twin-width) at most 3, even when a witnessing contraction sequence is given. Classes of bounded reduced component max-leaf (by any constant) and of twin-width at most 3 are known to exclude a fixed planar graph as an induced minor. The 3-Coloring and Feedback Vertex Set results refute more cases of the Gartland--Lokshtanov conjecture, even when the inputs are weakly sparse. The complexity of MIS in weakly sparse graphs excluding a planar induced minor remains open.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Glauber Dynamics for Sampling Colorings: Rapid Mixing above $(1+1/\mathrm{e})Δ$ via Hidden Hard-Core Models
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We show that for every $γ>0$ and every sufficiently large $Δ$, the Glauber dynamics for proper $q$-colorings of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $Δ$ has spectral gap $Ω_γ(1/n)$, and hence mixing time $O_γ(n^2\log q)$, whenever $q\ge(1+1/\mathrm{e}+γ)Δ$. Our proof establishes a Bochner-type inequality by exploiting the spectral gaps of hard-core models hidden in the color classes. The constant $1+1/\mathrm{e}\approx1.368$ comes from the uniqueness threshold $\approx\mathrm{e}/Δ$ of the hard-core model on the infinite $Δ$-regular tree.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$--$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries.
  For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 57 pages. v2: corrects cross-reference names (some lemmas, remarks, definitions and corollaries were labelled "Theorem"); no change in content

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Testing MAX-CUT in the Adjacency Matrix Model: Tight Non-Adaptive Bounds and a Cubic Adaptive Lower Bound
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the query complexity of approximating the MAX-CUT value to additive error $\varepsilon n^2$ in the adjacency matrix model. This was one of the first problems studied in graph property testing [GGR'98]. Previously, the best known upper bound for both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms was $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ [RV'07; MS'08; GMRS'22]. The only known lower bound was a trivial $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ bound. We close this gap from both sides for non-adaptive algorithms, proving that its query complexity is exactly $Θ(1/\varepsilon^4)$. We also prove an adaptive $Ω(1/\varepsilon^3)$ lower bound.
  Our upper bound is achieved by a canonical tester that samples $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ vertices in expectation and outputs the rescaled MAX-CUT value of the induced subgraph. We prove its correctness by applying spectral truncation to the adjacency matrix, using a geometric argument to control the sampling error of the retained low-rank part and a cut-norm restriction estimate [RV'07] for the remainder. As an application, an analogous proof also yields a tight $O(1/\varepsilon^4)$ non-adaptive query upper bound for MAX-2CSP.
  For our lower bounds, we show indistinguishability between a uniform random graph and a random graph with a planted hidden partition. For the non-adaptive lower bound, we observe that one plus the $χ^2$-divergence between the query transcript distributions is exactly a normalized Ising partition function, which can be bounded using Boolean hypercontractivity. For the adaptive lower bound, we relate each query's distinguishing power to the prediction, based on previous answers, of whether its endpoints lie in the same part of the hidden partition. We bound the combined advantage of these predictions using the completed transcript, which lets us analyze the adaptively chosen pairs of vertices together despite their dependence on earlier answers.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: First Near-Additive All-Pairs Approximate Shortest Paths in Decremental Weighted Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present the first four All-Pairs Approximate Shortest Paths (APASP) algorithms for decremental weighted undirected graphs. We extend the hierarchy induced edge sets of Baswana and Kavitha [FOCS'06 and SICOMP'10] to the decremental setting. At any point in time, for any $u,v$, $W_{i}$ denotes the weight of the $i$-th heaviest edge on any shortest path between them in the current graph.
  For any $\varepsilon>0$, our first algorithm maintains $(1+\varepsilon,2W_{2})$-APASP in $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{3}{2}+o(1)}m^{\frac{1}{2}})$ total update time, matching a single static computation of Cohen and Zwick [SODA'97 and JALG'01], up to a subpolynomial factor. It also improves the stretch of the $(2+\varepsilon)$-APASP algorithm of Dory, Forster, Nazari and de Vos [ICALP'24].
  Our second algorithm maintains $(1+\varepsilon,2W_{1}+2W_{2})$-APASP in $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{7}{3}})$ total update time, improving upon Chechik's $(3+\varepsilon)$-APASP algorithm [FOCS'18] for $m=Ω(n^{\frac{11}{6}})$.
  We also obtain two $(1+\varepsilon,2\cdot(k-1)W_{1})$-APASP algorithms with total update times $\tilde{O}(n^{2-\frac{1}{k}+o(1)}m^{\frac{1}{k}})$ and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+\frac{2}{3k-2}+o(1)})$, adapting the static $+2\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}W_{i}$-APASP algorithms of Cohen and Zwick [SODA'97 and JALG'01] and Roditty and Sapir [FSTTCS'25].
  For unweighted graphs, we present $(1+\varepsilon,2)$-APASP in $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{7}{3}})$ total update time and $(1+\varepsilon,2\cdot(k-1))$-APASP in $\tilde{O}(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k-4}+o(1)})$. Combined with the results of Dory, Forster, Nazari and de Vos [ICALP'24], these match the fastest combinatorial static bounds of Dor, Halperin and Zwick [FOCS'96 and SICOMP'00] up to subpolynomial factors.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/δ)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$.
  For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/δ)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 53 pages. Sharp asymptotic bounds unchanged. Strengthened fixed-class lower-bound construction, expanded technical overview, and clarified proofs

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Abelian embeddings make useful promises: approximation of detrivialised equations
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the following family of search problems: given a system of equations $x+y+z\equiv 0\pmod p$ promised to admit a solution that is nonconstant on every equation, find a $c$-colouring of the variables that makes no equation monochromatic. For $p\in\{2,3\}$, the problem recovers known tractable Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs). For $p > 3$, we obtain a complete complexity classification: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $c \geq 4$, yet even its decision version is NP-hard for $c = 3$, and it is not well-defined for $c = 2$.
  Our main conceptual contribution is a general tractability framework for PCSPs based on Abelian embeddings, a notion introduced by Bhangale, Khot, and Minzer [STOC 2022] in the study of quantitative approximation of satisfiable CSPs. We show that suitable Abelian embeddings yield polynomial-time PCSP reductions realised by singleton algorithms in the sense of Zhuk [FOCS 2026].
  On the hardness side, the promise relation is far removed from the reconfigurable regime covered by the conditional hardness framework of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima [LICS 2026]; our proof instead relies on a new additive-combinatorial rigidity theorem classifying special $3$-colourings of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$.
  Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(π_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Distributionally Robust Search: The Power of Information and the Limits of Moments
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study binary search for a target drawn from a distribution on $n$ ordered elements. The cost is the expected number of comparison queries. In our distributionally robust framework, the algorithm knows only an uncertainty set containing the distribution and minimizes its worst-case approximation ratio against an optimal strategy that knows the distribution. Collections of uncertainty sets capture different forms of information: quantiles, moments, general linear measurements, or approximate CDFs. This framework quantifies how much and what form of information is needed for near-optimal search.
  Our main result separates moments from general linear measurements. Although $n-1$ moments determine the distribution exactly, for every constant $δ\in(0,1)$, the first $n^{1-δ}$ exact moments can be as uninformative for search as no information: the worst-case approximation ratio remains $Ω(\log n)$. In contrast, for every constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $O(n^\varepsilon\log^4 n)$ suitably chosen linear measurements suffice for an $O(1/\varepsilon)$-approximation. The limitation lies in the measurements chosen, rather than linearity itself. Using LP duality and polynomial bounds of Rakhmanov and Bernstein, we construct distributions with identical moments and mass concentrated at different positions. For the upper bound, we combine dyadic sketches and Johnson--Lindenstrauss embeddings with a truncated median-search algorithm that converts uniform CDF approximation into search guarantees.
  Measuring information in bits, we prove a lower bound of $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ on the approximation ratio for summaries of any form using at most $\frac12 n^\varepsilon\log n$ bits, for every sufficiently small constant $\varepsilon>0$. Quantiles match this within constant factors. For Kolmogorov balls of radius $n^{-\varepsilon}$ the optimal approximation ratio is $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Constant-factor approximation of MinCostCSP with a conservative majority polymorphism
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For a relational structure A, the Minimum Cost Constraint Satisfaction Problem is the following problem denoted by MinCostCSP(A): Given an instance of CSP(A) with rational costs on variable-value pairs, find a solution to the instance minimizing the sum of the chosen costs. For the exact minimization, a classification of MinCostCSP(A) in terms of A was established by Takhanov [STACS'10].
  We focus on constant-factor approximations of MinCostCSP(A). DeHaan, Huang, and Lee recently showed that if A fails to admit a conservative near-unanimity polymorphism then MinCostCSP(A) is not constant-factor approximable [APPROX'25]. We provide a significant step towards a full classification, by proving a dichotomy for structures A admitting a conservative majority (also known as 3-near-unanimity) polymorphism. Our dichotomy criterion is not in terms of an algebraic condition on A but we show that this is unavoidable. We include a simple argument proving that no such condition exists.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact Tie-Breaking and Tight Degree Bounds for Minimum-Degree Greedy on Interval Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study tie-breaking in the minimum-degree greedy algorithm (MDG) for maximum independent set on interval graphs. Given an interval representation of an $n$-vertex graph, we compute the largest and smallest output sizes and construct executions attaining them in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n^2)$ space. For maximum degree at most four, favorable tie-breaking gives a tight guarantee of $3/4$. For every maximum-degree bound of at least five, the guarantee drops to $2/3$. Both bounds are tight even on connected unit interval graphs whose output size is independent of tie-breaking. Together with the known optimality of favorable tie-breaking for maximum degree at most three, these results give a complete classification by degree bound.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic Steiner Tree under Edge Updates
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Steiner tree problem is the canonical generalization of minimum spanning tree (MST). When connectivity is required only among a fixed subset of vertices (terminals), the goal is to maintain a minimum-cost tree connecting these terminals as the graph undergoes edge updates. While dynamic MST has been studied since the 1980s~[Frederickson, STOC'83, SICOMP'85], and the first sublinear-in-$n$ dynamic MST algorithm dates back almost thirty-five years to Eppstein, Galil, Italiano, and Nissenzweig~[FOCS'92, JACM'97], achieving sublinear-in-$n$ update time for dynamic Steiner tree has long remained open, as a single edge update can invalidate many routes in the underlying terminal metric closure.
  We present the first fully dynamic algorithm for Steiner tree that achieves a constant-factor approximation with sublinear-in-$n$ update time. For any fixed $0<ζ<1/2$, our deterministic algorithm maintains an $O_ζ(1)$-approximate Steiner tree for undirected graphs with polynomially bounded edge weights in $\widetilde O(n^{1/2+ζ})$ amortized update time, answering cost queries in $O(1)$ time, and reporting an explicit tree in $\widetilde O(n^{1+ζ})$ time. Our approach combines periodic terminal-metric rebuilds on a dynamic spanner with a top-tree dynamic program that localizes edge deletions and reconnects surviving components through a dynamic distance sparsifier. Along the way, we give a simpler randomized insertion-only algorithm with a better, explicit approximation ratio.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Polynomial-time Tensor Decomposition under the Kruskal Condition and the Lovitz--Petrov Generalization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
An identifiability criterion is a condition on a tensor decomposition that certifies uniqueness when the condition holds. Kruskal's classical condition is one of the best-known deterministic criteria for identifiability. However, no polynomial-time decomposition algorithm is known under the Kruskal condition; verifying the condition itself is NP-hard. Lovitz and Petrov introduced a strictly more general identifiability condition which, in contrast, is polynomial-time verifiable, but no polynomial-time decomposition algorithm was known under this condition either.
  In this paper we give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm, in the algebraic model over $\mathbb R$, for tensor decomposition under the Lovitz--Petrov condition, and therefore also under the stricter Kruskal condition.
  Moreover, combining our algorithm with polynomial-time verification of the Lovitz--Petrov condition yields an efficient end-to-end certification procedure: after computing a decomposition, one can deterministically certify in polynomial time that it is unique and therefore of minimum rank.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fully Scalable MPC Algorithms for Euclidean Clustering: Constant Approximation in Constant Rounds
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study Euclidean $k$-Means and $k$-Median under the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model, focusing on the \emph{fully scalable} setting. Previously, fully scalable algorithms for $k$-Means and/or $k$-Median either required $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$ rounds [Cohen-Addad, Kuhn, and Parsaeian; SODA'26] or guaranteed only an $O(\log n)$-approximation [Goranci, Jiang, Kiss, Kong, Qian, and Szilagyi; SODA'26]. In this paper, we close this gap by giving the first fully scalable algorithms for both problems, which work even when $k$ is polynomially larger than the local memory, and \emph{simultaneously} achieve an $O(1)$-approximation and $O(1)$ round complexity.
  Technically, we devise a new variant of the MP algorithm [Mettu and Plaxton, SICOMP'03] that computes a \emph{fractional solution satisfying the Lagrangian Multiplier Preserving (LMP) property}. Importantly, this LMP guarantee holds even under arbitrary distance distortions, a feature that is crucial for efficient MPC implementations. We then give a novel MPC rounding algorithm that first rounds to a bicriteria solution with $k+O(n^{1-ε})$ centers and then uses an \emph{iterative kernelization} idea to convert it into one with exactly $k$ centers.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Entropy-Weighted Soundness for Multi-Answer Birthday Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The vertices of a Boolean birthday graph are partial assignments on $\ell$-subsets of $n$ variables. Although a satisfying assignment induces a $K$-clique for $K=\binom n\ell$, an arbitrary selection of $K$ vertices may repeat some views and omit others. This makes soundness substantially harder than under uniform view sampling. For bounded-occurrence, constant-gap Boolean ternary CSPs whose constraints each involve three distinct variables (allowing arbitrary Boolean predicates), we prove that the graph's maximum induced $K$-vertex density satisfies \[
  ρ^*(K)\le 2\exp\!\left(-c\,
  \frac{\ell^3}{n^2\log(en/\ell)}\right) \] for $2\le\ell\le x_0n$ and $\ell\log(en/\ell)\ge C_0\log(n+1)$, with positive constants depending only on the source parameters. The argument refines the biclique counting method by charging the entropy of an adversarially chosen flattening to mutual information and a combinatorial obstruction energy. In the overlapping parameter range it strengthens the explicit soundness exponent previously established for this graph.
  We also establish an unconditional stability theorem for arbitrary sets $H$ of exactly $K$ distinct local assignments, with missing views and multiple answers: $f_*(H)\le34(n/\ell)q_{\mathrm{con}}(H)$ for every $1\le\ell\le n$. It gives a complementary additive near-clique soundness bound. We do not derive a new fine-grained hardness theorem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Binary Huffman Coding with Unequal Letter Costs Is NP-Complete
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Binary prefix coding assigns prefix-free binary words to symbols to minimize their frequency-weighted cost. Huffman solved the equal-letter-cost case in polynomial time in 1952 [Proc. IRE'52]. For unequal letter costs, Karp gave an integer-programming formulation in 1961 [IRE Trans. Inf. Theory'61].
